heroTitle: IB Career-related Programme Tutoring, Matched to How the CP Actually Works
heroSubtitle: The CP pairs IB courses with a career-related study and a reflective project, plus core components most schools mark on their own internal timeline. A tutor who has actually taught the CP knows the difference between DP rigor and CP's applied focus, and plans around it.
introSummary: Searching for IB Career-related Programme tutors usually means one of two things: a family new to the CP trying to understand how it differs from the Diploma, or a family already enrolled and stuck on the reflective project, a career-related study, or one of the core components. IB Gram matches students with tutors who have taught the CP specifically, not DP tutors filling a gap. Lessons run online worldwide in the family's own time zone, with home tutoring reviewed where a tutor is local, and hybrid plans for households that want both.

contentBlocks.heading: The CP's Own Shape, Separate From the Diploma Programme
contentBlocks.body: Schools that offer the IB Career-related Programme tend to run it alongside the Diploma Programme, not instead of it, and that shapes what a CP student actually experiences day to day. Two or three DP courses sit next to a career-related study chosen by the student — hospitality, engineering, design, business, health sciences, whatever the school partners with — and around that sit four core components: Personal and Professional Skills, Service Learning, Language Development and the Reflective Project. A school timetable built around the CP often assumes students can move between an academic classroom and a more applied, project-based one in the same week, and not every student adjusts to that switch on their own. Some schools are new to running the CP and are still working out their own internal deadlines for the Reflective Project and the career-related study portfolio, which means a family can find the school's own guidance thinner than it would be for a longer-established DP cohort. That gap is exactly where a subject-specific tutor earns their keep — not by replacing what the school teaches, but by making sure the reflective, evidence-based thinking the CP asks for is understood early, rather than rushed in the final term. IB Gram works with families in this position across many school systems, matching a tutor to the specific mix of DP subjects and CP core components a student has been set, not a generic IB package.

Four core components: Personal and Professional Skills, Service Learning, Language Development, Reflective Project
Two to three DP courses studied alongside the career-related study
School-set internal deadlines for the Reflective Project and portfolio evidence
Newer CP cohorts often have less established internal guidance than long-running DP cohorts

contentBlocks.heading: DP Subjects Most CP Students Pair With Their Career Study
contentBlocks.body: Most CP students take two or three Diploma Programme courses at Standard Level, chosen to support the career-related study rather than to build a full six-subject DP profile. A student on a business-focused career study might take Business Management and Mathematics; one on a health-sciences pathway might take Biology and Chemistry. Each of those DP subjects still carries its own internal assessment, still follows its own command terms and mark scheme, and still needs the same kind of steady, weekly attention a full DP subject would get — the CP does not make a Standard Level subject easier, it simply reduces how many a student carries at once. Tutoring on this page covers those paired DP subjects directly: IA structuring where the subject has one, past-paper practice mapped to the actual command terms an examiner is trained to mark against, and mock preparation timed to a school's own internal calendar rather than a generic exam countdown. Weekly goal setting matters more here than in a six-subject DP load, because a CP student often has less classroom time in each academic subject and less peer pressure to keep pace — a tutor who checks in weekly catches a slipping subject before a mock reveals it. One honest limitation: a tutor can strengthen a DP subject and the academic habits around the Reflective Project, but cannot substitute for the workplace exposure or industry partner relationship that the career-related study itself depends on — that part stays with the school and its partners.
items: IA structuring and mark-scheme technique for each paired DP subject
Past-paper practice organised by command term, not by topic alone
Mock exam preparation timed to the school's internal calendar
Weekly goal setting to catch a slipping subject early
Subject tutoring, not a substitute for the career study's workplace or industry component

contentBlocks.heading: How a Family Gets Matched to the Right Tutor
contentBlocks.body: A first request goes through a short review of what the student is actually studying: which DP subjects, which career-related pathway, whether the Reflective Project has a working topic yet, and what the school's own internal deadlines look like. That detail matters more for the CP than for most programmes, because two CP students at different schools can have almost nothing in common beyond the four core components. IB Gram uses that detail to shortlist tutors who have specifically taught CP students before, not DP or IGCSE tutors treated as interchangeable — subject depth checked against the actual course, and command-term familiarity checked against the actual assessment style the student will face. A first session is diagnostic rather than instructional: the tutor works through a recent piece of work or a past paper with the student to see where marks are actually being lost, then proposes a plan built around the weeks remaining before the next internal deadline or mock. Matching is not instant and depends on tutor availability for the subject and time zone requested; a family should expect a shortlist within a short window rather than same-day placement for a less common subject pairing. If the first tutor is not the right fit — pace, teaching style, or simply personality — a switch is reviewed rather than treated as a failure of the process, because getting this right matters more than getting it fast.
items: Initial review of DP subjects, career pathway and current Reflective Project stage
Shortlist built from tutors with direct CP teaching experience
Diagnostic first session using real student work or a past paper
Plan built around the school's own internal deadlines

contentBlocks.heading: Cities and Countries Families on This Page Are Writing From
contentBlocks.body: Families land on this page from a wide mix of places — some searching from cities such as Delhi, Bangalore, Chennai, Ahmedabad, Chandigarh, Coimbatore, Bhopal, Bhubaneswar, Dehradun, Faridabad, Ghaziabad and Greater Noida, others from international schools in entirely different countries running the same IB Career-related Programme under the same core components. What connects them is not geography but the programme itself: the same four core components, the same May and November examination sessions, the same reflective, evidence-based assessment style, whichever city or country the school sits in. Online tutoring is built for exactly this spread — a tutor in one city or country can work with a student in another, in the student's own time zone, without either side adjusting their day around travel. Home tutoring is reviewed case by case and depends on whether a tutor happens to be within reasonable travel of the student, which is realistic in some cities and simply not available in others; IB Gram does not promise a home tutor exists for every location, only that the option is checked when it is asked for. A hybrid arrangement — mostly online, with occasional in-person sessions where geography allows — is the middle path most families settle into once they see how the online sessions actually run. None of this depends on which curriculum board runs locally; the CP itself is set by the IB Organization and taught the same way regardless of the city hosting the school.

contentBlocks.heading: Four Core Components, Taken One at a Time
contentBlocks.body: The Reflective Project is the component families ask about most, because it is graded and sits closest to the Extended Essay in a DP cohort, without being the same task. It asks a student to investigate an ethical dilemma connected to their career-related study, and it is marked against criteria that reward genuine reflection and evidence of research process, not a polished final opinion. Academic honesty rules apply to it exactly as they do to DP coursework, and a tutor's job is to help a student build and reference an argument properly, never to shape the opinion itself. Personal and Professional Skills runs as a course over the length of the programme, usually assessed through a portfolio of tasks rather than an exam, and asks a student to reflect on real workplace or project experience — which means a tutor supports the writing and structuring, not the underlying experience. Service Learning has no exam at all; it is tracked through a school-approved log of activity and reflection, and the main risk is a student leaving it too late in the year rather than struggling with the content. Language Development asks for continued engagement with a second language at a level appropriate to the student, assessed through a portfolio the school reviews internally. None of the four core components is marked externally by written exam in November or May the way a DP subject is, but all four still run on the same academic-honesty and command-term expectations the IB applies across its programmes, which is why concept-based, evidence-led thinking matters even in components that look less exam-shaped on paper.

Personal and Professional Skills: portfolio-based, reflects on real experience
Service Learning: activity log and reflection, no exam
Language Development: portfolio-assessed continued language engagement

contentBlocks.heading: Checks Before a Tutor Ever Gets Matched
contentBlocks.body: Before a tutor is shown to a family, IB Gram checks subject background against the actual course being taught — not a general IB label, but the specific DP subject at the level the student is studying, plus direct experience with CP students specifically where the request is for CP support. A tutor claiming Reflective Project experience is expected to know the criteria the component is marked against and the difference between a reflective account and a merely descriptive one, because that distinction is where most students lose marks. Exam-board familiarity is checked against command terms — evaluate, discuss, analyse, to what extent — because a technically correct answer that ignores the command term still loses marks under IB criteria, and a tutor who cannot explain that difference is not matched to exam-preparation requests. Availability is confirmed for the time zone and days a family actually needs, not assumed from a general profile, since a tutor based in one region may simply not have evening slots that suit a student twelve hours away. None of this is presented as a guarantee of a particular grade or outcome — IB Gram does not offer either, and treats any claim of a guaranteed score as a reason to distrust a platform, not a reason to trust one. What is offered instead is a checked starting point: a tutor whose subject and component background genuinely matches the request, reviewed again after the first session rather than left unchecked once a match is made.

CP-specific experience checked separately from general DP experience

contentBlocks.heading: Online, Home or a Mix — What Actually Fits a CP Timetable
contentBlocks.body: Online tutoring is the default for most families using this page, and for the CP specifically it has a practical advantage: a student's career-related study can sit in an unusual niche — culinary arts, aviation, digital media — and the tutor best matched to a DP subject and comfortable with that pathway's demands may simply not live nearby. Online removes that constraint entirely, and sessions run in the family's own time zone rather than the tutor's. A stable connection and a quiet hour matter more for online CP tutoring than for younger students, because Reflective Project and portfolio work benefit from screen-sharing a live document rather than talking about it in the abstract. Home tutoring suits younger learners and families who prefer in-person structure, and it is reviewed against whether a tutor is realistically within a workable travel route — it is not offered as a default option everywhere, and a family should expect that honestly rather than assume it exists for every subject and city. Hybrid plans are common for CP students specifically: an online tutor for a DP subject that needs specialist depth, alongside an in-person arrangement for Reflective Project coaching if one is available locally. The trade-off to weigh honestly is that online tutoring demands more self-direction from the student between sessions — nobody is physically present to notice a distracted hour — while home tutoring costs more in travel time and is simply unavailable in a number of locations. Neither mode is presented here as universally better; the right one depends on the student's age, the subject's needs and what a family can actually sustain week to week.
items: Online default, especially for niche career-related pathways with no local specialist
Sessions run in the family's own time zone, not the tutor's
Home tutoring reviewed against realistic travel routes, not offered everywhere
Hybrid: online for subject depth, in-person for Reflective Project coaching where available

contentBlocks.heading: Working Alongside the School, Not Around It
contentBlocks.body: IB Gram is an independent tutoring platform and is not officially affiliated with the IB Organization, Cambridge International or Pearson Edexcel, and nothing on this page should be read as school-endorsed guidance — the school and its CP coordinator remain the authority on internal deadlines, the approved list of career-related study partners, and how Service Learning hours are logged and approved. A tutor's role sits alongside that structure, not above it: reinforcing a DP subject, helping a student plan and evidence the Reflective Project properly, and keeping momentum on core-component deadlines that a busy school term can otherwise let slip. Where a school runs the CP for the first time or with a small cohort, families sometimes find less peer support and fewer past examples to learn from than a large, established DP cohort would offer, and that is precisely where outside tutoring tends to help most — not by replacing the school's guidance, but by filling in what a small first-run cohort has not yet built up. A tutor should always be told what the school's own coordinator has already said about a component or deadline, so the two sources of guidance stay aligned rather than contradicting each other. Where they genuinely disagree — on interpretation of a criterion, say — the school's assessment stands, since it is the school that submits the moderated grade to the IB, not the tutor.
items: Independent platform: no affiliation with IB Organization, Cambridge or Pearson Edexcel
School's CP coordinator remains the authority on deadlines and approved pathways
Tutor role reinforces the school's teaching, does not replace it
First-run or small CP cohorts often benefit most from outside support
Where school guidance and a tutor's view differ, the school's assessment stands

contentBlocks.heading: Signs of Progress by Week Four
contentBlocks.body: By the end of four weeks, a parent should be able to point to something specific, not a general sense that lessons are happening. That usually means a completed diagnostic from the first session, a written plan tied to the student's actual DP subjects and Reflective Project timeline, and at least one worked example the student can explain back in their own words — the last of these matters most, because a student who can only repeat a tutor's explanation has not actually learned the command-term technique yet. Progress on the Reflective Project specifically should be visible as a working topic and a rough structure by week four, not a finished draft; the component rewards research process, and rushing a draft before the thinking is done tends to produce weaker reflective writing, not stronger. If none of that is visible after a month, the honest response is not to wait another month hoping it improves — it is to raise it directly and, if needed, request a different tutor. A mismatch is not a family's failure to manage tutoring correctly; it happens, and it is reviewed the same way a first match is reviewed, against subject background and teaching style rather than assumed to be the student's fault. Fees are set by tutor experience, subject, and session length rather than a flat platform rate, and a family should ask for that breakdown before committing to a term-length plan rather than after the first invoice arrives.
items: Completed diagnostic and written plan visible after session one
A worked example the student can explain independently, not just repeat
Reflective Project: working topic and rough structure by week four, not a finished draft
Mismatch reviewed and addressed directly rather than waited out
Fee breakdown requested before committing to a term-length plan

contentBlocks.heading: Starting a CP Tutoring Request
contentBlocks.body: Starting is straightforward: a parent shares the student's DP subject combination, the career-related pathway, the current stage of the Reflective Project if one has started, and the time zone or city the family is in. That detail shapes the shortlist far more than a general request for 'an IB tutor' would, because CP requests without subject and component detail tend to produce a slower, less accurate match. From there, a shortlist is reviewed against tutor availability, which varies by subject, level and season — availability tightens noticeably in the months before May and November sessions, so a request made early in a term has more options than one made two weeks before a mock. A first session is scheduled to diagnose, not to commit a family to a term immediately, and the plan that follows is built around the school's actual deadlines rather than a generic revision calendar. Families comparing tutoring options should ask direct questions before committing: has this tutor taught CP students before, what does a typical first month look like, how is progress reviewed, and what happens if the fit is wrong. Those questions matter more than any marketing claim, and IB Gram would rather a family ask them upfront than discover the answers after paying for a term. Submitting a request costs nothing and does not commit a family to anything beyond seeing who is actually available for their subject combination.
items: Share DP subjects, career pathway, Reflective Project stage and time zone
Shortlist reviewed against real tutor availability, tighter before May/November sessions
First session diagnoses fit; no term-length commitment required upfront

faqs.question: Is online tutoring actually effective for the CP's Reflective Project?
faqs.answer: Yes, for the writing and research-process side of it — screen-sharing a live document lets a tutor comment on structure and evidence in real time, which works as well online as in person for this kind of task. What online tutoring cannot do is replace the ethical-dilemma thinking itself; that has to come from the student's own experience with the career-related study. A tutor's role is to help structure and evidence a reflection the student has actually had, not to supply the reflection. Most families see this work well once the student is used to talking through drafts on a call rather than only in writing.

faqs.question: How much does IB Career-related Programme tutoring cost?
faqs.answer: Fees depend on the tutor's experience, the subject, and session length, and IB Gram does not publish one flat rate because CP requests vary too much to price generically — a specialist DP subject at Higher Level costs differently from general Reflective Project coaching. Ask for a clear per-session or per-month breakdown before committing to a term-length plan, and treat any platform quoting a single fixed price for every subject with some caution, since that usually means the price is not actually matched to what your child needs. A short diagnostic session is the right point to ask this question directly.

faqs.question: What if the first tutor isn't the right fit?
faqs.answer: It happens, and it isn't treated as a failure on the family's part. Raise it directly rather than waiting out a term hoping it improves — a mismatch in teaching style or pace rarely resolves on its own. IB Gram reviews the original request against subject background and availability again and proposes an alternative tutor. There's no penalty for asking for a switch after one or two sessions if something feels off; catching it early costs far less than persisting through a whole term with a tutor whose approach doesn't suit the student.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help if the school hasn't set a Reflective Project topic yet?
faqs.answer: Yes — this is actually one of the more useful times to start. A tutor can talk a student through how to choose a dilemma connected to the career-related study that's specific enough to investigate properly, rather than so broad it can't be argued with evidence. Waiting until a topic is assigned and then rushing the research afterward tends to produce weaker reflective writing. Starting the thinking process a few weeks before the topic is finalised, even informally, generally leads to a stronger first draft when the actual deadline arrives.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram offer home tutors for the Career-related Programme in every city?
faqs.answer: No, and it would be dishonest to claim otherwise. Home tutoring depends on a tutor being realistically available to travel to the student, which works in some cities and not in others, and CP-specific home tutors are less common than DP or IGCSE ones simply because fewer students take the CP. A request for home tutoring is reviewed rather than automatically fulfilled. Where no suitable home tutor is available, online tutoring is offered as the practical alternative, and most families find it works just as well for subject and core-component support.

faqs.question: What happens if a student shows no progress after a few weeks?
faqs.answer: First, that gets checked against something concrete — the written plan from the diagnostic session and whatever worked examples exist — rather than a general feeling. Sometimes the issue is pace, sometimes it's a mismatch between how the tutor teaches and how the student learns, and sometimes the plan itself needs adjusting once real classroom work is seen. Raise it with IB Gram directly rather than assuming nothing can be done; a plan review or a tutor change are both realistic next steps, and neither is treated as unusual.

faqs.question: Which DP subjects can be tutored alongside the career-related study?
faqs.answer: Any Standard Level DP subject a school allows within its CP structure, since the pairing is set by the school and the student's chosen pathway, not by IB Gram. Business Management, Mathematics, Biology, Chemistry, Economics and languages are common pairings with career studies like business, health sciences or hospitality, though the exact combination depends entirely on what the school offers. Tell IB Gram the specific subjects and level when making a request — the more precise this is, the faster and more accurate the tutor shortlist will be.

faqs.question: Are the exam sessions and deadlines the same everywhere?
faqs.answer: The IB's own May and November examination sessions are fixed globally, but the CP's core components are mostly assessed through school-set internal deadlines rather than a single external exam date, and those internal deadlines vary from school to school. That's one reason a generic revision calendar doesn't work well for CP tutoring — a tutor needs to know your school's actual dates for the Reflective Project and portfolio submissions, not just the IB's exam-session calendar, to plan sessions that arrive at the right point rather than too late or too early.

faqs.question: Is IB Gram affiliated with the IB Organization or with my child's school?
faqs.answer: No to both. IB Gram is an independent tutoring platform, not officially affiliated with the IB Organization, Cambridge International or Pearson Edexcel, and it has no relationship with any specific school beyond matching that school's students to tutors. The school's CP coordinator remains the authority on curriculum, internal deadlines and how components are marked and moderated. A tutor found through this page works alongside that structure, using the school's own guidance as the reference point, never replacing or contradicting it.

faqs.question: How does tutoring work for families far from their tutor's time zone?
faqs.answer: Sessions are scheduled in the family's own time zone, and a tutor's availability is checked against that before a match is confirmed, not assumed from a general profile. Families based far from most available tutors — a student in one region matched with a subject specialist several time zones away — usually settle into a regular weekly slot that suits both sides, often early evening for the student. It takes a short conversation to find a slot that holds up over a full term rather than working for one week and then falling apart.

heroTitle: Tutoring Built Around the IB Diploma, Not Just Exam Week
heroSubtitle: A tutor who understands HL and SL demands, internal assessment deadlines and the extended essay is different from one who only revises past papers in April. IB Gram matches families with subject tutors who can support the full two years, online worldwide or in person where a tutor is local.
introSummary: Looking for IB Diploma Programme tutors usually means one of two things: a subject is slipping mid-year, or May or November exams are close and past-paper practice has to start now. Either way, the right tutor understands HL and SL demands, internal assessment criteria and command terms, not just the syllabus content. IB Gram matches families with subject tutors for online lessons worldwide, in the family's own time zone, with home and hybrid options where a tutor happens to be local. Matching depends on subject, level and tutor availability — never guaranteed on the same day.

contentBlocks.heading: Firefighting Before Exams Versus Support That Runs All Two Years
contentBlocks.body:
Most enquiries about IB Diploma Programme tutors arrive in one of two moods: quietly proactive in September of Year 1, or genuinely worried three months before a May or November session. Both are legitimate reasons to start. But they need different kinds of support, and a page that pretends otherwise is not being honest with you.

Year-long support means a tutor who tracks internal assessment deadlines the school has already set, who knows the Extended Essay research question needs to firm up well before the second year begins, and who paces subject content against the syllabus rather than against whatever chapter feels urgent this week. Exam-season firefighting is narrower by necessity: past-paper technique, mark-scheme language, and triage of which topics still carry the most marks for the least remaining time.

Neither approach is wrong for its situation. A student six weeks from Paper 2 does not need a philosophical conversation about command terms; they need timed practice and specific feedback on where marks are being lost. A student starting Year 1 in September has the luxury of building habits — regular reading logs for Language A, consistent lab write-ups for the sciences — that make the last six months far less stressful.

What matters is telling a tutor, honestly, which situation this is. IB Gram asks that question in the first conversation, because it changes what the first month of sessions should look like.
items: Support from Year 1 IA proposals through to Year 2 mocks
Weekly goal-setting rather than one-off cram sessions
Coverage for both the May and November examination sessions
Continuity across TOK and CAS alongside subject content

contentBlocks.heading: Online, Home or a Mix — What Actually Fits a DP Timetable
contentBlocks.body:
DP students juggle more scheduling constraints than most: CAS commitments, IA deadlines spread across several subjects, sports or music alongside six subjects at HL or SL. So the question of online versus home tutoring is less about preference and more about what actually fits the week.

Online tutoring works well for most DP subjects because a screen-shared document does the same job a shared table used to. Higher Level Mathematics annotation, essay marking with tracked changes for Language A and B, even lab-report structure for the sciences — all of this transfers to a screen without real loss. It also opens access to a specialist tutor who may not live anywhere near the family, which matters for a subject like Higher Level Economics or a less commonly taught Group 6 elective where local specialists are thin.

Home tutoring suits a different case: a younger student who needs someone physically present to build study habits, or a family who simply concentrates better with a tutor in the room. It depends entirely on a tutor's travel range, though, and is never available on demand the way online sessions are — a fact worth knowing before assuming it will be there in a hurry.

Hybrid plans are the honest middle path many families land on: weekly online sessions to keep pace with the syllabus, with an occasional home or in-person session scheduled before a mock exam or an IA submission deadline, when working side by side genuinely helps. None of the three modes is superior in the abstract; the right one depends on the subject, the student's age, and the calendar.
items: Online: works across time zones, best for specialist HL subjects
Home: depends on a tutor's travel range in the family's city
Hybrid: weekly online sessions, home sessions before mocks or IA deadlines
Screen-sharing and shared documents replace the need for a shared table

contentBlocks.heading: What a DP Subject Tutor Actually Covers
contentBlocks.body:
The IB Diploma Programme organises subjects into six groups, and a tutor's usefulness depends on how well they know the specific group and level, not just 'IB' as a label. Group 1 and 2 cover Language A literature or language-and-literature, and Language B acquisition — tutoring here is about textual analysis, paper structure and the Individual Oral, not grammar drills alone. Group 3, Individuals and Societies, spans History, Economics, Psychology and Business Management, each with its own command-term conventions and source-evaluation criteria that a generalist tutor easily misses.

Group 4 sciences — Biology, Chemistry, Physics, Environmental Systems and Societies — carry both theory content and the internal assessment's scientific-investigation criteria, which reward a specific kind of write-up more than raw lab skill. Group 5 Mathematics splits into Analysis and Approaches and Applications and Interpretation, each offered at HL and SL with genuinely different demands; a tutor strong in AA HL is not automatically the right fit for AI SL. Group 6 electives and the arts sit alongside the DP core of Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS, which run through all three programme groups but need their own kind of support.

Exam preparation across Paper 1, 2 and sometimes Paper 3 depends on subject-specific mark schemes. Past-paper practice only helps when someone can explain why a mark was or wasn't awarded, which is a narrower skill than simply knowing the content.
items: Group 1 & 2: Language A and B, literary and linguistic analysis
Group 3: History, Economics, Psychology, Business Management
Group 4: Biology, Chemistry, Physics, Environmental Systems and Societies
Group 5: Mathematics AA and AI, HL and SL
Core: Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS

contentBlocks.heading: Where Home Tutoring Can Actually Be Arranged
contentBlocks.body:
Online tutoring for the IB Diploma Programme is available wherever a family has an internet connection and a time zone that a tutor can work around — that is the default, and it works for the overwhelming majority of subjects and levels. Home tutoring is a narrower offering by nature: it depends on a specific tutor's travel radius on a specific day of the week, not on a fixed office a family can simply visit.

In cities including Ahmedabad, Bangalore, Bhopal, Bhubaneswar, Chandigarh, Chennai, Coimbatore, Dehradun, Delhi, Faridabad, Ghaziabad and Greater Noida, some families have arranged home sessions when a tutor's own commute allows it. That list is illustrative, not a guarantee — availability shifts subject by subject and term by term, and a family in any of these cities may still be matched with an online-only tutor if that is who fits the subject and level best.

Traffic and school timings matter more for home sessions than most families expect before trying it. A tutor who can reach one part of a city easily by early evening may not be able to reach another part at all on a weekday, which is exactly why hybrid plans — online through the term, home sessions concentrated around a mock exam or an IA deadline — tend to work better than committing entirely to one mode from day one. IB Gram does not operate a branch address or walk-in centre in any city; every match happens directly between a family and a tutor, subject to that tutor's own schedule.
items: Online is the default and available wherever the DP is taught
Home sessions depend on a tutor's travel radius, not a fixed office
Sample cities with past home matches: Delhi, Bangalore, Chennai, Chandigarh
No walk-in centre — matching happens directly with a tutor

contentBlocks.heading: How the DP Fits Alongside MYP and IGCSE Transitions
contentBlocks.body:
Families arrive at the Diploma Programme from different starting points — some from the Middle Years Programme within the same school, others from an IGCSE curriculum with no MYP in between, and a smaller number transferring from a non-IB Year 11 entirely. Each transition carries its own adjustment, and pretending the DP simply continues where the previous programme left off undersells how different the assessment model actually is.

Concept-based learning means a tutor has to teach the 'why' behind a topic, not only the 'what', because DP exam questions are written to test transfer of understanding to unfamiliar contexts. Command terms carry real weight in the mark scheme: 'evaluate' and 'discuss' are scored differently from 'describe' or 'outline', and a student who answers a discuss question as though it said describe loses marks regardless of content knowledge. Academic honesty checks apply to every Internal Assessment and to the Extended Essay, which makes proper citation and process documentation part of the actual skill being taught, not an afterthought.

Criterion-related assessment is the other adjustment IGCSE transfers in particular tend to underestimate: DP subjects are marked against published criteria rather than a flat percentage scale, so understanding what each criterion actually rewards matters as much as content revision. A tutor who has taught the transition before — MYP to DP, or IGCSE straight into DP — usually gets a student oriented faster than one meeting the shift for the first time alongside the student.
items: Command terms like 'evaluate' and 'discuss' carry specific mark weight
Academic honesty checks apply to every IA and the EE
Criterion-related assessment replaces flat percentage marking
Transition support for students arriving from IGCSE or MYP

contentBlocks.heading: How a Tutor Match Actually Gets Made
contentBlocks.body:
Matching starts with specifics, not a general enquiry: subject, level (HL or SL), current or predicted grade if the school has issued one, and roughly how many weeks until the next assessment that matters — an IA deadline, a mock, or the May or November session itself. Vague requests get vague matches; specific ones get better ones.

Based on that, IB Gram reviews tutors for subject-matter background and familiarity with the DP syllabus and command-term conventions at that level, then offers a short-list rather than a single take-it-or-leave-it option, so a family can choose based on a short conversation or a brief trial.

The first session is diagnostic, not instructional in the traditional sense: it covers where the syllabus currently stands, what the IA or EE looks like if one is underway, and which past-paper areas are weakest. Out of that comes a written plan — topic sequence, target dates, and what 'progress' should look like in four weeks, which is deliberately concrete rather than a vague promise of improvement.

Week four is a genuine review point, not a formality: has the plan been followed, has the weak area actually moved, and does the tutor-student working relationship feel right. If any of that answer is no, changing tutors at that point is normal and expected, not a failure of the process — a mismatch found early costs far less than one carried for two years.
items: First session: diagnostic review of syllabus gaps and IA/EE status
Week two: a written plan with topic sequence and target dates
Week four: progress review against the plan, tutor change if needed
Ongoing: session notes shared after every class

contentBlocks.heading: What We Do Not Promise, and What We Check Instead
contentBlocks.body:
It is worth saying plainly what this page will not promise: no guaranteed grade, no promised 7, no invented improvement percentage, and no tutor headcount presented as a credibility signal. Anyone offering a guaranteed outcome for an externally examined, criterion-marked qualification is either overstating what tutoring can control or hasn't thought carefully about what actually determines a DP result — prior preparation, effort, school support and the exam itself all play a part that no tutor fully owns.

What can be checked, and is checked before a match is offered, is more specific: the tutor's subject-matter qualification, relevant teaching or exam-marking background where it exists, and demonstrated familiarity with DP command terms and the specific subject's mark scheme rather than IB terminology in general.

Fees are not fixed platform-wide; they depend on subject, level, session frequency and the individual tutor, and should be confirmed in writing before the first paid session, not assumed from a headline number seen elsewhere.

One honest limitation deserves saying directly: a tutor starting two months before a May session cannot substitute for two years of accumulated syllabus gaps. Focused past-paper work in that window can lift technique and confidence meaningfully, but it cannot rebuild content that was never taught or retained the first time. Families weighing a late start are better served knowing that ceiling upfront than discovering it in April.
items: Subject qualification and exam familiarity checked before matching
No score or grade guarantees — outcomes depend on effort and starting point
Fees depend on subject, level and frequency, confirmed before starting
A late start narrows what is realistically achievable before the exam session

contentBlocks.heading: Where the DP Is Taught, and Why IB Gram Stays Independent of It
contentBlocks.body:
The Diploma Programme is delivered by IB World Schools across many countries, and each school sets its own internal calendar within the IB's overall timeline — its own IA submission dates, its own mock exam weeks, its own CAS reporting checkpoints. A tutor working around 'the DP schedule' in the abstract is working around nothing useful; what matters is the specific school's calendar, which a tutor needs from the family directly rather than assuming a generic template applies.

This also means tutoring has to flex around term breaks, school event weeks and exam block schedules that vary from one school to the next, sometimes significantly, even within the same city or the same examination session.

IB Gram is an independent tutoring platform. It is not affiliated with the IB Organization, with Cambridge International, or with Pearson Edexcel, and it does not claim partnership with any specific school anywhere in the world. Tutors are matched to a family's stated subjects, level and school-set deadlines — never presented as representing a school or the IB Organization in any official capacity.

That independence cuts both ways, worth naming honestly: it means no institutional access to a school's specific assessment criteria beyond what is publicly documented by the IB, so a tutor's guidance is built on general DP assessment knowledge and the student's own school-issued materials, not privileged information from inside any school.
items: Each school sets its own IA and mock deadlines inside the IB timeline
Tutoring schedules built around the student's own school calendar
IB Gram is independent of the IB Organization, Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel
No claim of partnership with any specific school worldwide

contentBlocks.heading: The Checks Before a Tutor Ever Meets a Student
contentBlocks.body:
Verification happens before a tutor is ever offered to a family, and again on an ongoing basis afterward — it isn't a one-time badge that gets stale. The first stage is identity and qualification documentation: proof of the degree or teaching credential claimed, and evidence of the subject background relevant to the specific DP subject and level being taught, since a general science background is not the same as demonstrated Higher Level Chemistry depth.

The second stage is subject-specific screening rather than a generic interview: familiarity with the actual command terms and mark-scheme language for that subject, awareness of the internal assessment criteria that apply, and, where relevant, exam-familiarity built from having actually taught or marked similar work before.

After a match begins, feedback from the family after the first few sessions feeds back into whether that tutor continues to be offered for similar requests — a tutor who consistently gets flagged for pacing issues or unclear explanations gets reviewed, not left on the list by default. This is closer to an ongoing quality loop than a single gate at onboarding.

None of this is presented as infallible. A qualification document and a good first impression cannot fully predict classroom chemistry between a specific tutor and a specific teenager, which is exactly why the week-four review exists as a real checkpoint rather than a formality.
items: Identity and qualification documents reviewed before listing
Subject-specific screening matched to HL/SL demands
Parent feedback collected after the earliest sessions
Tutors reviewed periodically, not only at onboarding

contentBlocks.heading: Start With One Diagnostic Session
contentBlocks.body:
Starting is deliberately simple, and it should stay that way: a parent describes the subject, the level, the current grade situation and how urgent the timeline is, and that's the information a match is built from — nothing more elaborate is needed at this stage.

From there, expect a short-list of tutors rather than a single option, a first session that functions as a diagnostic rather than a full lesson, and a written plan coming out of that session with actual dates on it. None of this happens instantly in every case; matching is subject to tutor availability for that specific subject and level, and a rare or advanced combination — a less common Group 6 elective at HL, for instance — may take a little longer to match well than a widely taught subject like English A or Mathematics AA.

Families in a genuine hurry, three or four weeks from an exam session, should say so upfront rather than mentioning it after a plan is already built around a slower timeline; it changes what the first session should prioritise. Families starting in September have more room to build the kind of habits that make the following May easier, and that is worth saying honestly too, since it is the better time to start whenever a school calendar allows it.
items: Tell us the subject, level and current grade
Get matched with a short-list of tutors, subject to availability
First session covers a diagnostic and a written plan
Review progress at week four, adjust or switch if needed

faqs.question: Can one tutor cover both HL and SL versions of the same subject?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, though it depends on the tutor. HL and SL share a core syllabus in most Group 3–5 subjects but diverge in depth, option topics and paper structure — HL Mathematics AA, for instance, adds calculus depth that SL never touches. A tutor confident across both levels can usually adjust, but if a student is genuinely borderline between HL and SL, or considering switching mid-year, say so early. That decision affects pacing, IA expectations and which past papers are actually useful, so it changes what the first month of tutoring should focus on.

faqs.question: Is online tutoring really enough for something like Higher Level Mathematics?
faqs.answer: For most students, yes — annotation tools and shared working let a tutor walk through calculus or statistics exactly as they would at a table, and HL Maths tutoring is mostly about worked method and technique rather than physical materials. It suits a student comfortable working from a screen. It suits it less well if a student needs someone physically present to stay focused, in which case a home or hybrid arrangement, where a tutor is locally available, tends to work better than forcing online sessions that aren't landing.

faqs.question: My child's Internal Assessment is already behind schedule — can a tutor help before the May session?
faqs.answer: Often, yes, though what's realistic depends on how far behind and in which subject. A tutor can help restructure the remaining IA timeline, clarify what the criteria actually reward, and triage which sections need the most attention with the time left. What a tutor cannot do is submit work on a student's behalf or guarantee the school will accept a late resubmission — that decision sits with the school, not with IB Gram. Starting the conversation with the school early, alongside tutoring, matters more the further behind the IA already is.

faqs.question: Does tutoring cover the Extended Essay separately from regular subject lessons?
faqs.answer: Yes, EE support is usually arranged as its own thread even when the same tutor also teaches the subject, because EE supervision runs on a different timeline — research question refinement, source evaluation and the reflections process happen alongside, not inside, regular syllabus lessons. A tutor experienced in supervising EEs in that subject area understands the assessment criteria and the academic-honesty documentation the IB requires, which is different knowledge from teaching subject content itself, so it's worth confirming a tutor has done both before assuming one covers the other.

faqs.question: How is the fee structured for IB Diploma Programme tutoring?
faqs.answer: There's no single platform-wide rate — fees depend on the subject, whether it's HL or SL, the tutor's own experience level, and how many sessions a week the plan involves. A family should get a clear figure confirmed in writing before the first paid session, not an estimate that shifts afterward. It's reasonable to ask directly what a specific tutor charges and how that compares before committing, and IB Gram expects that question rather than treating it as awkward.

faqs.question: What happens if the tutor isn't the right fit after we've started?
faqs.answer: Switching is normal, and the week-four review exists partly to surface exactly that question honestly rather than let a mismatch drag on for months. If pacing feels wrong, explanations aren't landing, or the working relationship simply isn't clicking, saying so leads to a new match rather than a refund argument or an awkward continuation. A mismatch caught in week four costs a few sessions; one carried silently for a full term costs far more, in both time and a student's confidence.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram support both the May and November examination sessions?
faqs.answer: Yes — matching and past-paper preparation run for both sessions, since school cohorts sit in May or November depending on their calendar and hemisphere. What differs is the preparation timeline relative to when a family starts: a student in a November-session school starting tutoring in September has a shorter runway than one starting the previous January, and that timeline should shape the plan from the first session rather than being treated as a minor detail.

faqs.question: We don't live near a major city — is home tutoring even an option?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on whether a suitable tutor's travel range reaches that specific location, which isn't guaranteed outside cities with a larger tutor base. Online tutoring is the reliable fallback in that situation, and for most DP subjects it works just as well as an in-person session would. It's worth asking directly during matching rather than assuming either way — sometimes a tutor's travel route covers an area that wouldn't seem obvious from the city name alone.

faqs.question: How does a tutor follow my child's specific school's syllabus rather than a generic IB outline?
faqs.answer: By asking for it directly in the first session — the school's own scheme of work, past assessment papers if the school shares them, and the specific IA and mock deadlines that school has set. The IB publishes a common subject guide, but how a school sequences topics, when it runs mocks, and which past papers it favours varies enough that a tutor working from a generic outline alone will drift out of step with actual classroom pacing within a few weeks.

faqs.question: What actually happens in the first session before we commit to ongoing lessons?
faqs.answer: The first session is a diagnostic, not a full lesson: the tutor reviews where the syllabus currently stands, checks IA or EE progress if applicable, and identifies the two or three weakest areas from recent past-paper attempts or school assessments. Out of that comes a short written plan with a rough timeline, which the family reviews before deciding whether to continue. There's no long-term contract signed at that point — the plan itself is what's being agreed to, not a fixed term.

introSummary: IB Middle Years Programme tutors help students aged roughly eleven to sixteen keep pace with concept-based units, command-term language and criterion-related assessment across whichever subject groups need attention — Sciences, Mathematics, Language and Literature, Individuals and Societies, Arts, Design, PE and Health, or Language Acquisition. IB Gram matches your child with a tutor who already teaches to MYP criteria, not a generalist adapting on the fly. Sessions run online in your family's own time zone, with home tutoring available where a tutor is genuinely local, and hybrid arrangements for families who want both. Matching depends on subject, grade and tutor availability.

contentBlocks.heading: The Scheduling Problem Before the Subject Problem
contentBlocks.body: Before you compare tutors on subject expertise, sort out the timetable — because for the IB Middle Years Programme, timing kills more tutoring arrangements than teaching quality ever does. A student in MYP might have six or seven subject groups running concurrently, each with its own homework rhythm, plus co-curricular commitments a school timetable rarely leaves room to move. Add a tutor in a different time zone and a session that looked fine on a shared calendar app quietly becomes a 6 a.m. call nobody wants to keep. So the honest first question isn't 'who is the best tutor for Sciences' — it's 'when, realistically, can this happen every week without one side resenting it.' Online tutoring solves most of this cleanly: sessions run in the family's own time zone, so a Tuesday evening slot stays a Tuesday evening slot regardless of where the tutor is based. Home tutoring is different. It depends entirely on whether a tutor's travel route reasonably includes your address, and school-day traffic in most cities makes an evening home session harder to hold than an online one at the same hour. Hybrid plans — home sessions when the calendar allows, online the rest of the time — are common for families who want in-person contact without demanding it every week. None of this is a reason to delay. It is a reason to decide mode before subject, because mode decides whether the plan survives past week three.

contentBlocks.heading: Eight Subject Groups, Not One Syllabus
contentBlocks.body: The Middle Years Programme is built from eight subject groups — Language and Literature, Language Acquisition, Individuals and Societies, Sciences, Mathematics, Arts, Physical and Health Education, and Design — and a tutor who is strong in one is not automatically useful in another, because MYP assessment criteria differ by subject group even when the underlying skill looks similar. A Sciences tutor works against criteria for knowing and understanding, inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating, and reflecting on the impacts of science; a Language and Literature tutor works against analysing, organising, producing text and using language. Command terms — analyse, evaluate, justify, discuss — carry specific weight in MYP marking, and a tutor who treats 'discuss' the way a different curriculum would is setting a student up to lose marks on structure rather than content. Interdisciplinary units, which combine two subject groups around a single concept, are another place generalist tutoring falls short — they need a tutor who understands both disciplines' criteria well enough to help a student connect them rather than answer for each separately. In MYP year five, many schools also run the Personal Project, a long independent piece of work assessed against its own criteria, where the tutor's job is closer to structured coaching on planning and reflection than subject teaching. Matching by subject group, not just 'MYP' as a blanket label, is what actually determines whether a session helps.
items: Sciences: inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating criteria
Language and Literature: analysing, organising, producing text criteria
Command terms like 'discuss' and 'evaluate' carry specific MYP weight
Interdisciplinary units need cross-criteria understanding, not two separate tutors
Personal Project (MYP5) needs planning and reflection coaching, not subject drilling

contentBlocks.heading: Where MYP Sits Between PYP and the Diploma
contentBlocks.body: MYP is the middle stretch of the IB continuum, and it helps to place it there rather than treat it as a standalone exam course, because the skills it builds are the ones the Diploma Programme and Career-related Programme later assume are already in place. The Primary Years Programme, before it, is inquiry-led and largely ungraded; MYP introduces criterion-related assessment, command terms and formal academic honesty expectations for the first time, which is exactly why the transition into MYP1 or MYP2 catches some students off guard even when they were doing well in PYP. What comes after — DP or CP — assumes a student can already structure an extended response, cite sources correctly and manage internal-assessment-style deadlines without being told each step. A tutor working with a MYP student well is quietly preparing them for that jump, not just clearing this term's homework. Age bands within MYP are programme-specific rather than fixed by a single grade label across every school, since some schools run a five-year MYP and others a shorter version ending earlier, so it is worth confirming with the school which year of MYP a child is actually in before booking anything. On-screen eAssessment, where a school opts into it for the final year, adds a further layer — typing speed, on-screen annotation and exam-interface familiarity become real preparation items. For those schools, timed past-paper practice under on-screen conditions is usually the single most useful activity, more useful at that stage than extra content review.
items: PYP before MYP: inquiry-led, largely ungraded
MYP introduces criterion-related assessment and command terms
DP/CP after MYP assume structured, cited, deadline-driven work
Age bands are programme-specific — confirm the exact MYP year with the school
Optional on-screen eAssessment rewards timed past-paper practice, not just content review

contentBlocks.heading: Online, Home or a Mix — What Actually Fits
contentBlocks.body: Online tutoring is the default for most MYP families simply because it removes the single biggest constraint — geography — and opens up specialist subject tutors regardless of which city or country a family is in. For a subject group with fewer strong local tutors, such as a less common Language Acquisition option or higher-level Design, online is often the only way to find someone genuinely qualified rather than settling for whoever happens to be nearby. Home tutoring suits younger MYP students, particularly in MYP1 and MYP2, where a parent wants a tutor physically present to manage focus and pacing, and it works best when the tutor's travel route reasonably includes the family's address — arranging it purely on hope rather than checked logistics usually fails within a month. Hybrid plans are the middle path: a weekly online session for steady subject work, with an occasional in-person session before a big test or when a concept genuinely needs a whiteboard and shared paper rather than a screen. None of the three modes is objectively 'better' — the honest trade-off is that online maximises subject-matching and home maximises in-person presence, and a family choosing between them is really choosing which of those two things matters more this term. Availability for any mode is subject to which tutors are free at the time you enquire, not a guarantee attached to the mode itself.
items: Online: widest specialist choice, fixed to the family's time zone
Home: better for younger MYP students, needs a realistic travel route
Hybrid: weekly online plus occasional in-person before assessments
No mode is universally better — it's a trade-off, not a hierarchy
All modes remain subject to tutor availability at enquiry time

contentBlocks.heading: How a Tutor Gets Matched to Your Child
contentBlocks.body: Matching starts with specifics, not a general request for 'an MYP tutor' — subject group, MYP year, current school, what the last report card actually said, and whether the concern is a specific unit, exam technique, or a broader confidence problem. That detail is what separates a useful match from a random one, because two students both labelled 'struggling with MYP Sciences' can need completely different tutors — one needs criterion-by-criterion exam technique, the other needs the underlying concept explained a second time in different words. IB Gram uses that information to shortlist tutors who teach that specific subject group at that specific level, rather than offering the first available tutor with 'IB' on their profile. A first session is treated as diagnostic on both sides: the tutor checks where the gaps actually are against MYP criteria, and the parent and student check whether the working style fits — pace, tone, how much the tutor pushes versus explains. Neither side is committed based on that one session. If the fit is wrong, the honest and normal outcome is a second match, not persevering for a term out of politeness, since a mismatch that continues rarely resolves on its own and mostly wastes the weeks it runs for. Weekly one-to-one sessions, fees and mode are confirmed once both sides are satisfied, not before.
items: Match request specifies subject group, MYP year and current gap
Shortlist built from tutors teaching that exact subject and level
First session is diagnostic — checks fit, not a locked-in commitment
A poor fit is re-matched, not persisted with out of politeness
Fees and schedule confirmed only after both sides agree on fit

contentBlocks.heading: Families Doing This From Very Different Places
contentBlocks.body: An MYP family arranging tutoring through IB Gram could be based in Ahmedabad, Bangalore, Bhopal, Bhubaneswar, Chandigarh, Chennai, Coimbatore, Dehradun, Delhi, Faridabad, Ghaziabad or Greater Noida — or in a country altogether outside that list, since IB World Schools run on every continent and the platform is not tied to any single market. What matters for matching is time zone and mode, not the city name itself. Two families in different cities with children in the same MYP year and the same subject group gap can end up with the same shortlist of online tutors, because the tutor's specialism and the student's actual need line up regardless of geography. Where the difference shows up is home tutoring: that option only exists where a tutor is genuinely local enough to travel reliably, so a family in a smaller city, or a less-served part of a larger one, may find online is the more realistic route even if home was the original preference. This is worth saying plainly rather than glossing over — home tutoring is not universally available everywhere IB Gram operates, and a parent should ask directly whether a home-capable tutor exists for their specific subject and area before planning around it. Online removes that uncertainty entirely, which is part of why most MYP matches end up running that way by default rather than by second choice.
items: Time zone and mode decide the shortlist, not the city name
Same subject-group gap in different cities can get the same tutor shortlist
Home tutoring exists only where a tutor can travel reliably
Smaller or less-served areas often default to online for that reason
Ask directly whether a home-capable tutor exists before planning around it

contentBlocks.heading: What Gets Checked Before a Tutor Is Introduced
contentBlocks.body: A tutor profile that says 'IB experienced' means very little without specifics behind it, so the checks that matter are concrete: which subject group and which MYP years the tutor has actually taught, whether that included criterion-related assessment and internal moderation rather than only exam coaching, and whether they can explain command terms the way a school actually marks them rather than in general terms. Academic background is checked against the subject group claimed — a tutor teaching MYP Individuals and Societies should have a background that supports it, not an adjacent subject stretched to fit. Availability and realistic schedule capacity are confirmed before a match is offered, so a family isn't introduced to someone who technically qualifies but cannot actually hold a weekly slot. None of this produces a public rating or a review score — IB Gram does not publish tutor ratings or invented statistics, and any claim that sounds like a guaranteed grade outcome should be treated as a red flag regardless of which platform it comes from, since no honest tutor can promise a specific IB result. What a parent should reasonably expect instead is transparency about what was checked and why a particular tutor was shortlisted for this specific subject group and year. Questions about a tutor's background are answered plainly before the first session is booked, not deflected.
items: Subject group and MYP years actually taught are checked, not assumed
Background verified against the specific subject group claimed
Realistic weekly availability confirmed before a match is offered
No published ratings, no invented statistics, no guaranteed-grade claims
Questions about a tutor's background are answered before booking

contentBlocks.heading: How This Fits Around an IB World School's Calendar
contentBlocks.body: Every IB World School sets its own internal deadlines for coursework, mock assessments and unit tests inside the broader May and November IB examination session calendar, and tutoring that ignores those dates is tutoring that arrives too late to help. A tutor working well with an MYP student asks for the school's assessment calendar early — when is the next Sciences unit test, when is an Individuals and Societies essay due, when does the school run its own mock week — and builds sessions backward from those dates rather than working through a generic syllabus at a flat pace. Academic honesty is treated with the same seriousness a school applies to it: a tutor helps a student understand and structure their own work, not produce it for them, because MYP moderation checks for exactly that and a student who submits tutor-written work risks the assessment being invalidated entirely. IB Gram is an independent tutoring platform. It is not affiliated with the IB Organization, Cambridge International, Pearson Edexcel, or any individual school, and it does not have access to a school's internal systems, grades or assessment records — a parent remains the point of contact with the school for anything official, and tutoring supplements that relationship rather than replacing any part of it. Where a school runs its own criteria slightly differently from the general MYP framework, the tutor adapts to the school's version, not the reverse.
items: Tutoring built backward from the school's own assessment calendar
Academic honesty respected — coaching structure, not producing the work
IB Gram is independent, not affiliated with the IB Organization or any school
No access to a school's internal systems, grades or records
Tutor adapts to the specific school's version of MYP criteria

contentBlocks.heading: What Four Weeks Should Actually Look Like
contentBlocks.body: By the end of four weeks, a parent should be able to point to something specific that changed — a criterion the student previously misunderstood and now applies correctly, a command term they no longer confuse with another, a piece of homework completed with less back-and-forth than it needed a month earlier. Vague reassurance that 'things are going well' without a concrete example is worth questioning, not accepting at face value. A reasonable first-session structure covers where the student currently sits against the relevant MYP criteria, what the next school deadline is, and a short revision plan for the weeks between now and it — not a generic 'let's see how it goes' opening that wastes a paid session on discovery that could have happened over a message beforehand. Progress in MYP is genuinely slower to see than in an exam-heavy curriculum, because criterion-related assessment rewards depth over a term rather than a single test score, and a parent expecting weekly grade jumps will be disappointed regardless of tutor quality — that is a fair limitation to name rather than paper over. What should be visible instead is the student's own account of what they now understand that they didn't before, and whether homework and unit tests are landing with less last-minute scrambling. If neither is true by week four, that is the moment to raise it directly rather than waiting out the term.
items: A specific criterion or command term corrected, not vague reassurance
First session maps current standing against criteria plus the next deadline
MYP progress shows over a term, not a weekly grade jump — a real limitation
Student's own account of new understanding is a useful signal
Raise it directly at week four if nothing has actually changed

contentBlocks.heading: Starting Without Overcommitting
contentBlocks.body: None of this requires a term-long commitment signed on day one. The reasonable way in is a single diagnostic session against the subject group and MYP year that actually needs attention, reviewed honestly afterward by both the tutor and the parent before agreeing to anything ongoing. That review should cover whether the tutor's explanation style matched how the student learns, whether the pace felt right for the time available before the next deadline, and whether continuing weekly makes sense given the school calendar ahead — May and November examination sessions on one end, and each school's own internal deadlines running throughout the year on the other. Fees, frequency and mode — online, home or hybrid — get confirmed once that first session has actually happened, not guessed at in advance based on a generic price list, because what a subject and level actually need varies enough that a flat number rarely reflects what a family will really use. If a first match doesn't fit, saying so and asking for a different tutor costs nothing but a short conversation, and it is the normal next step, not an awkward one. Starting small and correcting quickly beats committing broadly and hoping it works out.
items: Start with one diagnostic session, not a term-long commitment
Review fit honestly before agreeing to anything ongoing
Fees and frequency confirmed after the first session, not guessed upfront
A poor first match is simply re-matched — no penalty for asking
Build the schedule around May/November sessions and school deadlines

faqs.question: Is online tutoring actually effective for the IB Middle Years Programme, or does a subject like Sciences need someone in the room?
faqs.answer: For most MYP subject groups, online works well because the tutor can share a screen, annotate mark schemes and work through command terms just as directly as in person — Language and Literature, Individuals and Societies and Mathematics translate especially well. Sciences and Design sometimes benefit from hands-on elements a screen can't replicate, such as lab technique or physical prototyping, which is where a hybrid plan with occasional in-person sessions makes more sense than pure online. The honest limitation: if a subject genuinely needs physical materials every week, online alone will underserve it, and that's worth naming before committing rather than discovering it a month in.

faqs.question: What happens if the tutor and my child just don't click?
faqs.answer: That's treated as normal, not a failure on either side. If the first session shows a mismatch in pace, tone or explanation style, say so and ask for a different tutor rather than continuing out of politeness — a mismatch rarely improves with time and mostly costs weeks that matter against school deadlines. A second match is arranged based on what specifically didn't work the first time, which usually narrows the fit considerably. There's no penalty or awkward process for asking; it happens often enough in MYP matching that treating it as exceptional would be dishonest.

faqs.question: How much does IB Middle Years Programme tutoring cost?
faqs.answer: Fees vary by subject group, MYP year, tutor experience and whether sessions are online, home or hybrid, so there isn't one flat number that means anything without those specifics. IB Gram confirms fees once a match is made and the mode of tutoring is agreed, rather than quoting a price before knowing what a family actually needs. As a general pattern, home tutoring tends to cost more than online because of travel time, and specialist subjects with fewer available tutors can sit at a different rate than more commonly taught ones. Ask for specifics against your child's exact subject and year.

faqs.question: My child is starting MYP1 having come from a non-IB school. How much catching up is realistic?
faqs.answer: It depends heavily on which subject groups the previous school covered and how differently they assessed work, more than on how 'behind' the student seems on day one. The biggest early adjustment is usually not content but format — command terms, criterion-related assessment and the expectation of structured, cited responses are often new regardless of prior school quality. A tutor familiar with that transition focuses the first few weeks on format and expectations rather than racing through content, which tends to close the gap faster than drilling subject material the student may already understand well enough.

faqs.question: Is IB Gram affiliated with the IB Organization or with my child's school?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram is an independent tutoring platform and is not affiliated with the IB Organization, Cambridge International or Pearson Edexcel, and it has no access to any school's internal systems, gradebooks or assessment records. Tutors are matched based on subject, MYP year and experience with the relevant criteria, but the school remains the only authoritative source for grades, deadlines and official communication. Tutoring is meant to support what the school is already doing, not to stand in for it or to claim any official status it doesn't have.

faqs.question: Can one tutor cover multiple MYP subjects, or does my child need a different tutor for each?
faqs.answer: A tutor can reasonably cover more than one subject group if their background genuinely supports both — Mathematics and Sciences overlap often enough for this to work, for instance — but stretching a single tutor across unrelated groups like Design and Language Acquisition usually means one subject gets weaker coverage than the other. It's more honest to match by strength than to bundle for convenience. Families needing help across several subject groups sometimes end up with two or three tutors on a shared weekly schedule rather than one generalist, which tends to produce better results per subject.

faqs.question: What does the MYP Personal Project involve, and can a tutor actually help with it?
faqs.answer: The Personal Project, typically completed in the final year of MYP, is an independent piece of work a student plans, develops and reflects on against its own assessment criteria, separate from any single subject group. A tutor's role here is coaching, not content delivery — helping the student structure a realistic timeline, understand what the reflection criteria actually expect and avoid the common trap of an overly ambitious goal set too late to finish well. Because it's assessed on process as much as outcome, a tutor who tries to shape the product too heavily can undermine the academic honesty the project depends on.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram offer home tutoring in my area?
faqs.answer: That depends on whether a tutor for your child's specific subject group happens to have a travel route that reasonably includes your address — it isn't guaranteed everywhere IB Gram operates. Ask directly when you enquire, giving your area and subject, and you'll get a straight answer about whether home tutoring is realistic or whether online is the more dependable option for that combination. Many families who start by asking for home tutoring end up choosing online anyway once they see it removes the travel-time constraint entirely and widens the subject-matched shortlist considerably.

faqs.question: How do IB exam sessions affect when we should start tutoring?
faqs.answer: IB examinations run in May and November, but most of what affects MYP scheduling is internal — unit tests, mock weeks and coursework deadlines each school sets on its own calendar within that broader cycle. Starting tutoring reactively, right before a deadline, limits what's realistically achievable to exam technique and last-minute clarification. Starting several weeks ahead of the school's own internal assessment dates allows time to actually address a misunderstood criterion or command term rather than just rehearsing answers. Ask your child's school for their internal calendar before agreeing on a tutoring start date.

faqs.question: What if there's no real progress after a couple of months?
faqs.answer: Raise it directly and specifically — which criterion or command term still isn't landing, and what the tutor has tried so far — rather than assuming tutoring in general doesn't work. Sometimes the fix is a different tutor with a different teaching style; sometimes it's a change in frequency or mode, such as adding a short home session before a school test. MYP progress is genuinely slower to see than in exam-only curricula because criterion-related assessment rewards depth over a term, but two months with no visible change in understanding is a fair point to reassess rather than wait out further.
