h1: IB Primary Years Programme Tutors: What Actually Helps at This Age
heroTitle: IB Primary Years Programme Tutoring, Built Around How Young Learners Actually Work
heroSubtitle: For children roughly 3 to 12, in the PYP's inquiry units, a tutor's job is narrower than parents expect: build confidence, close specific skill gaps, and support the unit of inquiry your child's teacher has set, not run a parallel curriculum alongside school.
introSummary: Most parents come to IB Primary Years Programme tutors assuming the PYP works like exam-based programmes further up the school, with content to drill and papers to practice. It doesn't. PYP has no external exams; assessment sits inside each unit of inquiry, judged against criteria the class teacher sets. A tutor who understands that spends less time on worksheets and more time helping a child ask better questions, structure an explanation, and manage the open-ended tasks PYP favours. IB Gram matches families worldwide with tutors experienced in exactly this kind of support, online or, where available, in person.

contentBlocks.heading: The Assumption That Trips Up Most PYP Parents
contentBlocks.body: Ask a parent why they are looking for IB Primary Years Programme tutors and the answer is often the same one: 'exam season is coming' or 'we want extra practice papers.' Neither applies here. The PYP, for children roughly aged 3 to 12, runs on internal, criterion-based assessment tied to units of inquiry, not external papers with a May or November sitting. There is no Paper 1 or Paper 2 to revise for at this stage. What trips families up is applying the DP mental model — content coverage, past papers, grade targets — to a programme built around concept-based learning, command terms used in a very different way, and academic honesty expectations that show up even at age eight, in how a child cites where an idea came from during a unit of inquiry. A tutor who treats PYP like a smaller DP will hand a nine-year-old worksheets when what the child actually needs is help structuring a response to an open-ended inquiry question, or building the vocabulary to explain their thinking clearly. That mismatch is common, and it is fixable early. The better question to ask a prospective tutor is not 'how many past papers do you have' but 'how do you support a child through an inquiry cycle, and how do you talk to a class teacher about what the unit actually requires.' Get that right and the rest of the support tends to follow naturally.
items: No external exams in PYP — assessment is internal and criterion-based
Units of inquiry, not fixed syllabus content, drive what gets taught
Academic honesty expectations start as early as age 7-8
Command terms work differently in PYP than in MYP or DP
A DP-style 'past papers' request is usually the wrong ask

contentBlocks.heading: Where In-Person and Hybrid Support Can Actually Reach
contentBlocks.body: IB Primary Years Programme tutors work with families in very different situations — a family posted abroad with school starting at 7:30am local time, a household in a hub city wanting someone to sit with their child twice a week, another wanting a purely online arrangement so a specialist in a particular language of instruction can be involved. Online tutoring is available worldwide and runs in the family's own time zone, which matters more for younger children than adults sometimes assume: a session scheduled against a child's natural energy dip, right after a long school day, rarely goes well regardless of how good the tutor is. Home tutoring depends on a tutor's actual travel radius, so it is realistic in some hub cities and not others. Among the hub cities where a home or hybrid arrangement may be reachable, depending on the specific tutor and neighbourhood, are Bangalore, Chennai, Delhi, Ahmedabad, Bhopal, Bhubaneswar, Chandigarh, Coimbatore, Dehradun, Faridabad, Ghaziabad and Greater Noida — though reach within any of these still comes down to which pocket the tutor already covers, not the city as a whole. Outside these, online is the default, and for PYP-aged children it is not a compromise: a specialist tutor available on a screen twice a week for 45 minutes is usually a better outcome than an available generalist tutor who happens to live nearby.

contentBlocks.heading: Online, Home, or Something Between: Matched to the Child's Age
contentBlocks.body: The right mode changes more with age than most other factors. A six-year-old often needs a parent or another adult in the room for an online session — not to teach, but to keep focus and handle the technology — while an eleven-year-old close to the PYP exhibition can usually run an online session independently and prefers the flexibility. Online tutoring gives access to specialist subject tutors regardless of city, which matters when a family needs someone comfortable with a particular language of instruction or a specific inquiry-based teaching style their school uses. Home tutoring suits younger learners and families near a tutor's existing travel route; it also suits children who genuinely concentrate better away from a screen, which is a real and fairly common pattern at this age, not a preference to be talked out of. Hybrid plans combine both — a fortnightly home session for hands-on project work, with shorter online check-ins in between for reading practice or homework support. None of these is inherently better. The honest trade-off: home tutoring costs more in a tutor's travel time and limits the pool of available tutors to whoever can reach the address; online removes that limit but asks more of the child's independent focus, which is exactly why a parent's own read of their child matters more here than in later programmes.
items: Younger children (roughly 3-7) often need an adult present for online sessions

contentBlocks.heading: Literacy, Numeracy and Inquiry Skills a PYP Tutor Actually Works On
contentBlocks.body: PYP does not divide into exam subjects the way later programmes do, but a tutor still needs real subject depth. Literacy work covers reading comprehension, writing structure and the specific vocabulary a unit of inquiry introduces — a unit on 'Sharing the Planet' brings its own words a child needs to use accurately, not just recognise. Numeracy work builds through strands like number, pattern, measurement and data handling, usually tied back to whatever real-world context the current unit is exploring. Beyond these two anchors, tutoring support can extend into the transdisciplinary units themselves: helping a child research a topic, organise findings, and present them the way a PYP unit of inquiry expects, which is a genuinely different skill from answering a worksheet question. Academic honesty applies here too — a tutor should be showing a child how to say where information came from, not doing the research for them. Assessment support in this age range means helping a child understand what a rubric or set of success criteria is actually asking for, practising the specific skill an upcoming assessed task will test, and building toward the PYP exhibition in the final year, which is a sustained, student-led inquiry project rather than a single test. None of this looks like conventional exam coaching, and a tutor who tries to make it look that way is usually solving the wrong problem.

Numeracy: number, pattern, measurement, data handling strands
Research and presentation skills for transdisciplinary units
Understanding rubrics and success criteria, not just answers
Sustained support toward the PYP exhibition in the final year

contentBlocks.heading: Step by Step: How a Match Gets Made
contentBlocks.body: The process starts with a short conversation about the child, not the subject — age, the specific unit of inquiry or skill area causing difficulty, school timings, and whether the family wants online, home or hybrid support. That detail shapes which tutors even get considered, since a tutor experienced with five-year-olds and one experienced with eleven-year-olds close to their exhibition are rarely the same person. IB Gram then proposes tutors whose background fits: experience with the PYP specifically, comfort with concept-based and inquiry-led teaching rather than pure content delivery, and availability that actually matches the family's schedule rather than a best-effort guess. A first session is treated as a genuine trial, not a formality — the tutor should come away from it with a clear sense of the child's reading level, number sense, and confidence talking through their thinking out loud, and the parent should come away with a plan for the next few weeks, not a vague reassurance. Around the four-week mark, a short review looks at concrete signs: is the child attempting inquiry tasks more independently, has reading stamina or number fluency actually moved, is the child asking better questions in class. If a match is not working, changing tutors is a normal part of the process, not an admission of failure by either the family or IB Gram — the goal is fit, and fit sometimes takes two attempts to find, especially at an age when personality matters as much as subject knowledge.

Tutors proposed based on PYP-specific and age-specific experience
First session treated as a genuine trial, not a formality
Four-week check looks at concrete, observable signs of progress

contentBlocks.heading: Connecting PYP Support to MYP and Beyond
contentBlocks.body: PYP is the first of the IB's continuum, and the habits it builds — structuring an inquiry, managing an open-ended task, explaining reasoning rather than just stating an answer — carry directly into the Middle Years Programme that follows, and eventually into the Diploma Programme's IA and EE work years later. A tutor who understands this continuum handles a PYP session differently: less concerned with covering more content faster, more concerned with building the underlying skill an MYP criterion or later a DP internal assessment will eventually demand. This matters practically for families with children at different stages — a household with a Year 5 PYP student and an older sibling starting MYP benefits from tutors who at least understand how the two connect, even if they are not the same tutor for both children. It also matters when a family is deciding how much to invest in PYP-stage tutoring at all: skills built now in structuring an argument or handling an open-ended task are not wasted the moment a child moves up, the way memorised content sometimes is. That is a reasonable argument for starting PYP support earlier rather than later, but it is not a reason to over-schedule a young child — two focused sessions a week generally serve a PYP-aged learner better than a heavier timetable borrowed from an older sibling's programme.

Structuring inquiry and reasoning matters more than content recall

contentBlocks.heading: Working Alongside an IB World School, Not Instead of It
contentBlocks.body: A PYP tutor's job sits next to the school's programme, never in place of it. The unit of inquiry, the assessment criteria, and the pace of the curriculum are all set by the child's own IB World School, and a tutor who ignores that in favour of an outside syllabus is working against the child's actual timetable rather than for it. In practice this means a tutor should be asking to see the current unit planner, or at least understand its central idea and lines of inquiry, checking in on how the school's own assessment tasks are structured, and adjusting session content week to week as the school's unit changes — PYP units typically run for several weeks before rotating to the next one. IB Gram is an independent tutoring platform and is not officially affiliated with the IB Organization, Cambridge International or Pearson Edexcel, and it has no relationship with any specific school a family's child attends. That independence is deliberate: it means a tutor's first loyalty is to what actually helps the child inside their own school's programme, not to a separate curriculum being sold alongside it. Families should expect a tutor to ask questions about the school's expectations rather than arrive with a fixed plan already decided before that conversation happens.

contentBlocks.heading: Vetting a Tutor Before They're Introduced to Your Child
contentBlocks.body: Before a tutor is put in front of a family, several things get looked at, and it is worth being specific about what, rather than gesturing at 'vetting' as a word. Academic background is checked against the age range and subject areas the tutor claims to cover — teaching six-year-olds and coaching an eleven-year-old through an exhibition draft call for different experience, and both get checked separately rather than treated as interchangeable. Familiarity with the IB's own language matters too: whether a tutor can talk comfortably about units of inquiry, transdisciplinary themes, and criterion-related assessment, or whether they are translating everything from a more traditional, content-first frame of reference. Prior experience with PYP-aged learners specifically is weighted more heavily than general tutoring experience, since managing a young child's attention and confidence is a distinct skill from explaining content clearly. References and background information are reviewed as part of onboarding. None of this produces a guarantee — no vetting process can promise a personality fit between a specific tutor and a specific child — but it does mean a family is choosing from tutors who have already been checked against the actual demands of this programme and this age group, rather than a general pool of subject tutors with no PYP-specific screening at all.

Familiarity with PYP-specific language: inquiry, transdisciplinary themes, criteria
PYP-specific experience weighted above general tutoring experience

contentBlocks.heading: No Guaranteed Outcomes, and What Can Be Said Honestly Instead
contentBlocks.body: It would be easy to promise a fixed number of reading levels gained or a guaranteed jump in confidence by a certain date, and plenty of tutoring services do exactly that. IB Gram will not, because PYP does not produce the kind of scored outcome that makes such a promise meaningful — there is no grade to guarantee, no percentile to point to. What can be said honestly: matching depends on tutor availability at the time a family enquires, and a strong fit sometimes takes a session or two to confirm rather than being obvious immediately. Progress at this age also depends on things a tutor cannot control — how much reading happens at home between sessions, how a child is coping with the rest of their school day, whether an assessed task genuinely interests them. A tutor can build skill and confidence; a tutor cannot substitute for a child's own engagement with school life. One honest limitation worth naming directly: tutoring works less well for a child who is disengaged from school generally rather than struggling with one specific skill, and in that situation a conversation with the school's own teacher usually matters more than adding a tutor. Families are better served by that honesty upfront than by a promise that quietly assumes conditions outside anyone's control.

Availability is real and depends on which tutors are free at the time

contentBlocks.heading: Getting Started This Week
contentBlocks.body: Starting is simpler than most families expect once the earlier confusion about exams and content is cleared up. It begins with naming the actual concern precisely — not 'my child needs a PYP tutor' in general, but 'my child is struggling to structure written responses during their current unit of inquiry' or 'we want support ahead of the exhibition next term.' That specificity is what lets a tutor be matched well rather than generically. From there, a short intake conversation covers age, current unit or skill focus, school timings and time zone, and preferred mode — online, home where a tutor is reachable, or hybrid. A trial session follows, with a clear check afterward: did the tutor understand the child's actual level within the first twenty minutes, did the child engage rather than tolerate the session, is there a concrete plan for the next few weeks. Scheduling should work around school hours and family life, not the other way round — two well-timed sessions a week generally beat three squeezed into an already tired evening. Availability is subject to which tutors are free in a given time zone and, for home or hybrid arrangements, which tutors already travel near the family. None of this needs to be decided in one sitting; a single trial session is a reasonable, low-commitment way to see whether a specific tutor is the right fit before agreeing to anything longer.

faqs.question: Does the IB Primary Years Programme even have exams that need tutoring?
faqs.answer: No. PYP has no external examinations — assessment happens inside each unit of inquiry, judged against criteria the class teacher sets, plus a sustained student-led exhibition in the final year rather than a written test. Because of that, tutoring for PYP looks different from exam coaching: less past-paper practice, more work on structuring an inquiry response, building reading and number fluency, and preparing for the exhibition itself. If a tutor's plan for your child leans heavily on drilling exam-style questions, that is usually a mismatch with how PYP is actually assessed, worth raising directly before the first session.

faqs.question: What age does IB Primary Years Programme tutoring start, and is it worth it for a 5- or 6-year-old?
faqs.answer: PYP covers roughly ages 3 to 12, and tutoring can start anywhere in that range, though what it looks like changes a great deal. For a 5- or 6-year-old, a session is usually short, playful and built around reading confidence or early number sense rather than formal instruction, often with a parent nearby. It's worth it when a specific gap is visible — reluctance to read aloud, discomfort with basic number work — rather than as a general precaution. Starting this early is less about content and more about building comfort with learning itself.

faqs.question: Does online tutoring actually work for a child this young, or does it need to be in person?
faqs.answer: It can work well, with a caveat: younger children generally need an adult nearby to manage focus and technology during an online session, which is different from needing the adult to teach. Sessions also need to be shorter and more interactive than they would be for an older student — twenty to thirty minutes, not a full hour, often works better. For children closer to 10 or 11, online sessions are usually manageable independently. Home tutoring remains a reasonable choice for a child who concentrates better away from a screen; that's a real pattern, not something to overcome.

faqs.question: How does IB Gram find a tutor when we're not sure which subject area needs the most help?
faqs.answer: That's a normal starting point, not a problem. The initial conversation asks about what you're actually observing — reluctance to read, difficulty explaining thinking out loud, trouble with a specific type of number problem — rather than asking you to name a subject area precisely. A proposed tutor's first session then functions as an assessment in itself, checking reading level, number fluency and confidence talking through ideas, which usually clarifies where the real gap sits within the first session or two, before any longer-term plan gets built around it.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with the PYP exhibition in the final year?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it's one of the more common requests for older PYP students. The exhibition is a sustained, student-led inquiry project, so a tutor's role is support rather than direction: helping a child narrow a broad topic into a workable inquiry question, plan research steps, organise findings, and rehearse how they'll present, without taking over the thinking the exhibition is meant to demonstrate. Tutors experienced with this stage understand the line between helping a child structure their own work and doing the work for them, which matters for a task built around academic honesty.

faqs.question: What happens if the tutor and my child don't get along?
faqs.answer: You change tutors — that's a normal, expected part of the process, not a failure on anyone's side. Personality fit matters more at PYP age than in later programmes, since a young child's engagement depends heavily on liking the person across the screen or table from them. If a first session or two isn't working, say so plainly rather than persisting out of politeness; a new tutor can be proposed based on what specifically didn't click, whether that was pace, teaching style, or simply personality, so the next match starts from better information.

faqs.question: How much does IB Primary Years Programme tutoring cost?
faqs.answer: Fees vary by tutor experience, the mode chosen — online generally costs less than home tutoring once a tutor's travel time is factored in — and how many sessions a week the family wants. There's no single fixed rate to quote here, since it depends on the specific tutor matched to your child's age and needs. What's worth asking upfront is the per-session rate, whether it changes for hybrid arrangements, and what a trial session costs before committing to an ongoing schedule, so there are no surprises once sessions are underway.

faqs.question: We're moving between IB World Schools mid-year — can a tutor help with that transition?
faqs.answer: Yes, this is a genuine use case, since PYP schools can differ in pacing, unit sequencing and how strictly they follow the same central ideas even under one shared framework. A tutor can help a child catch up on vocabulary or skills the new school assumes but the previous one hadn't yet covered, and just as usefully, can help a child understand how the new school's expectations around inquiry work or assessment criteria differ from what they're used to. This matters more for a mid-unit move than a move between school years.

faqs.question: What should we expect to see after about four weeks of sessions?
faqs.answer: Concrete, observable signs rather than a vague sense of improvement: a child attempting inquiry tasks with less prompting, reading with more stamina or fluency, showing improved number confidence in the specific strand being worked on, or asking sharper questions during class discussions their school teacher may also notice. If none of that is visible after four weeks, that's a signal to review the match itself rather than assume more time will fix it — sometimes it's pace, sometimes it's fit, and both are worth naming directly rather than waiting quietly.

faqs.question: Is IB Gram affiliated with the IB Organization or with our child's school?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram is an independent tutoring platform and has no official affiliation with the IB Organization, Cambridge International or Pearson Edexcel, and no relationship with any specific school your child attends. Tutors work to your own school's unit planner and assessment criteria, not a separate curriculum, and are expected to ask about your school's specific expectations before proposing a plan. That independence means a tutor's priority is what actually helps inside your child's existing programme, not a competing syllabus sold alongside it.

contentBlocks.heading: How to Compare Two IGCSE CP Tutors Properly
contentBlocks.body: Two tutors can look identical on paper — same degree, same years of experience, same claimed familiarity with Cambridge or Pearson Edexcel — and still be a poor match for very different reasons. The comparison that actually matters happens on three points, not one. First, has this tutor taught the specific subject inside the Career-related Programme your child is taking, at the right grade band, recently? Second, do they understand how CP work is assessed alongside the IGCSE subject itself — the applied project, the reflective component, the way a school or exam board weighs both? Third, can they commit to a schedule that survives a busy term, not just the first two weeks of enthusiasm. A tutor who scores well on subject knowledge but has never touched the CP's non-exam assessment side will teach the content correctly and still leave the applied-learning piece thin. A parent comparing two shortlisted names should ask each one, directly, what a first session would cover and what they would check in week four. The answer tells you more than any credential list. IB Gram's matching process is built around these same three points rather than a generic profile match, because a mismatch discovered in month two costs far more than a slightly longer shortlisting conversation in week one. This is the shortlisting work IB Gram does before a name reaches you at all.

contentBlocks.heading: Subject Combinations Inside the Career-related Programme
contentBlocks.body: The Career-related Programme is built around one core idea: an IGCSE subject sits alongside applied, career-related coursework, and both halves get assessed on their own terms. That mix is exactly why generic subject tutoring falls short here. A tutor might be excellent at teaching the IGCSE content in isolation and still have no framework for the coursework planning, the reflective writing, or the mark-scheme technique the applied side actually needs. IB Gram does not publish one fixed subject list for this programme, because CP combinations vary by school and by student — what matters is matching a tutor to the specific subject your child is studying and to the applied component that sits next to it. In practice that support covers coursework and internal-assessment planning from the first weeks of a term, structured past-paper practice against the Cambridge or Pearson Edexcel syllabus, and mark-scheme technique so a student learns to write answers examiners actually reward, not just answers that are technically correct. Mock preparation is built in ahead of internal and external checkpoints, and sessions run against a weekly goal rather than a vague revision plan, so a family can see concrete movement between one month and the next. If your child's combination pairs a subject IB Gram has less common request volume for, that is disclosed honestly during matching rather than papered over — availability is confirmed before a first session is booked, not assumed.

contentBlocks.body: A request starts with four pieces of information: the subject inside the Career-related Programme, the grade band, whether the target sitting is the May/June or October/November series, and the preferred mode — online, home or hybrid. That is enough for a first shortlist. Tutors are matched on recent experience with this exact subject at this level, not a broad 'IGCSE tutor' label, because CP support depends on understanding both the subject content and how the applied component is assessed alongside it. A shortlist includes tutors whose availability actually fits the family's week, since a perfect subject match with no compatible slot is not useful to anyone. Once a tutor is selected, the first session is diagnostic rather than instructional: it establishes where the student stands against the syllabus, what has been covered in school, and where the gaps sit before a plan is built. Parents are usually on that first call, or briefed immediately after it, so expectations are set before four or five sessions have already happened. From there, sessions run to a plan the tutor sets out in writing — not a vague 'we'll see how it goes' — with checkpoints tied to the exam session ahead. If the match is not working after a few sessions, a different tutor can be brought in without restarting the paperwork — that flexibility matters more in CP, where the wrong pairing costs real project time, not a wasted hour.

contentBlocks.heading: Where Families Are Tutoring From
contentBlocks.body: IB Gram works with families in more than fifteen countries, and for the Career-related Programme specifically, most of that support runs online — a subject tutor in one city, a student in a different time zone entirely, meeting on a fixed weekly slot that both sides commit to. Home tutoring requests do come from specific cities, though, and among the ones IB Gram sees regularly for this programme are Ahmedabad, Bangalore, Bhopal, Bhubaneswar, Chandigarh, Chennai, Coimbatore, Dehradun, Delhi, Faridabad, Ghaziabad and Greater Noida — alongside plenty of others, since CP is offered by schools well beyond any single cluster of cities. Where a home tutor is requested, availability depends entirely on whether a suitable subject specialist is actually based within reasonable travel of the student, which is a real constraint and not a formality — a strong tutor two hours away by traffic is not a workable home match. This is where online tutoring genuinely outperforms the alternative: a family is not limited to whichever specialists happen to live nearby, and scheduling can be built around the family's own evening rather than a tutor's commute. Hybrid arrangements — a home session every week or two, online sessions filling the gaps — tend to work well for families who want in-person contact occasionally without making it the only option. None of this changes the subject-matching standard; it only changes how the session is delivered once a tutor is confirmed.

contentBlocks.heading: IGCSE Sitting Alongside a Career-related Qualification
contentBlocks.body: The Career-related Programme is structured differently from a standard IGCSE subject run on its own, and that structural difference is worth understanding before choosing a tutor, not after. IGCSE tutoring in this context works to published Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel syllabus objectives, assessment objectives and mark schemes — the same rigorous baseline as any other IGCSE subject. What changes is what sits alongside it: applied, career-related study that is assessed on its own criteria and often carries coursework or a reflective project component with deadlines that do not move for exam-board convenience. Missing a coursework deadline because a tutor only tracked the syllabus content is a completely avoidable failure, and it happens more often than families expect when a tutor is hired purely for subject knowledge. The two Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel exam series — May/June and October/November — set the external rhythm, but the internal deadlines for career-related coursework typically fall well before either sitting, sometimes months earlier depending on the school's own calendar. That earlier deadline is easy to lose track of amid exam-focused revision, and it is exactly the kind of detail a subject-only tutor can miss. IB Gram's matching brief for CP specifically flags this dual timeline so a tutor plans backward from both dates, not just the one that is easier to see coming. Getting this sequencing wrong costs weeks that cannot be recovered close to a sitting.
items: IGCSE subject content assessed to Cambridge or Pearson Edexcel objectives
Career-related coursework assessed on separate criteria
Internal coursework deadlines usually fall before the exam series
May/June and October/November series set the external rhythm
Tutors plan backward from both deadlines, not just the exam date

contentBlocks.heading: Checks Run Before a Tutor Is Listed
contentBlocks.body: Every tutor matched for the Career-related Programme is checked against the same short list of criteria before a name is ever shown to a family. Subject-specific teaching background is verified, not just a general education degree — a tutor listing this subject needs to show they have actually taught it, not adjacent content that sounds similar. Familiarity with the relevant exam board, Cambridge or Pearson Edexcel, is checked separately, because mark-scheme conventions differ enough between boards that general subject knowledge does not automatically transfer. Identity and background checks are run before a tutor is approved to take live students at all, and this step is treated as non-negotiable regardless of how strong a tutor's academic profile looks otherwise. References or prior tutoring history are reviewed where available, and a tutor's actual teaching approach is discussed directly during onboarding rather than inferred from a CV. None of this is presented as a guarantee of outcome — no tutoring arrangement can promise a specific grade, and any platform claiming otherwise is not being straight with you. What verification actually buys a family is confidence that the person sitting across from their child, in person or on a screen, is who they say they are and can teach what they say they can teach. That is a lower bar than a marketing page implies, and also the only one that is honestly checkable before a first session happens.
items: Subject-specific teaching background verified, not just a degree
Exam-board familiarity checked separately (Cambridge vs Pearson Edexcel)
Identity and background checks before live students
References and tutoring history reviewed where available
Teaching approach discussed directly during onboarding

contentBlocks.heading: Online, Home or a Mix of Both
contentBlocks.body: Online tutoring for the Career-related Programme works because it removes the single biggest constraint on subject matching: geography. A family in one time zone can work with a subject specialist in another, provided the weekly slot is fixed and both sides treat it as non-negotiable — a session that moves every week rarely survives a full term. Screen-sharing a past paper, annotating it live, and reviewing coursework drafts in real time cover most of what CP support needs; the applied and reflective components take written feedback well between sessions. Home tutoring suits a different situation: a younger student who needs someone physically present to hold focus, or a family that specifically wants in-person accountability for coursework deadlines. It depends entirely on a suitable tutor being based close enough to make the arrangement practical — a genuine limitation, since a strong exam-board specialist is not guaranteed to live within travel range of every student. Hybrid plans split the difference: a home session for the parts that benefit from being in the room together, usually deadline-heavy coursework check-ins, and online sessions for regular content coverage and past-paper practice. None of the three modes changes what a tutor is expected to deliver. The choice is about which format the family and student will actually show up to, consistently, for the length of a full term — because the best-matched tutor in the world cannot help a session that keeps getting rescheduled.
items: Online removes geography as a constraint on subject matching
Home tutoring suits younger students or deadline-heavy accountability
Home availability depends on a specialist being locally reachable — a real limitation
Hybrid pairs a home session with online continuity
A fixed weekly slot matters more than the mode chosen

contentBlocks.heading: Working Around Your School's Own Timetable
contentBlocks.body: Schools running the Career-related Programme set their own internal calendar for coursework submission, mock assessments and progress reviews, and that calendar rarely lines up neatly with a generic tutoring schedule built around the exam series alone. A tutor who only tracks the May/June or October/November sitting can miss a school's internal deadline that falls three months earlier, which is exactly the deadline that actually determines whether the coursework component is complete. Because of this, matching for CP specifically asks what a student's school requires internally, not just what the exam board eventually asks for, and a tutoring plan is built to sit alongside the school's own timetable rather than compete with it. This matters more around school assessment weeks and mock periods, when a student's time is genuinely limited and a tutor needs to know what has already been asked of them that week rather than adding a parallel workload on top. IB Gram is an independent tutoring platform and is not officially affiliated with the IB Organization, Cambridge International or Pearson Edexcel, and no school partnership is claimed or implied anywhere on this page — tutors are matched to what a student's own school and syllabus require, using information the family provides directly. Where a school communicates specific coursework criteria or a marking rubric, that document is the reference point in sessions, not a tutor's general assumption about what 'usually' gets marked well.
items: Internal coursework deadlines often precede the exam series by months
Tutoring plan built around the school's own calendar, not just the exam date
IB Gram is independent — no affiliation with IB Organization, Cambridge International or Pearson Edexcel
School-issued marking rubrics used as the reference point in sessions
Extra load avoided during school assessment and mock weeks

contentBlocks.heading: The One-Month Progress Check
contentBlocks.body: By the end of four weeks, a family should be able to point to something specific, not a general sense that sessions are 'going fine.' That specific thing might be a Paper 1 style question completed inside the allotted time, a coursework draft that has come back tighter after one round of feedback, or a topic that has moved from a consistent blank to merely shaky. If none of that has happened by week four, that is worth raising with the tutor, not waiting out quietly in the hope it resolves itself. A reasonable tutor will have a specific answer about what changed and what is planned for weeks five through eight; a vague answer at that point is itself useful information. What should not be expected in four weeks is a transformed grade trajectory — genuine subject gaps take longer than a month to close, and any platform implying otherwise is overselling what tutoring can actually do. What four weeks can reasonably show is direction: is the student's independent work improving, are past-paper scripts showing fewer of the same repeated errors, is the coursework on schedule against its own internal deadline. Those are checkable facts, not impressions, and a parent should ask for them directly rather than accepting reassurance as a substitute. If the answer to all three is no, changing tutors at that point costs less than waiting another month to be sure.
items: A concrete skill or habit change by week four, not a vague impression
Ask what changed and what's planned for weeks five to eight
Genuine subject gaps take longer than a month to close
Track direction: independent work, repeated errors, coursework schedule
Switching tutors early costs less than waiting another month

contentBlocks.heading: Starting With a Single Session
contentBlocks.body: There is no obligation attached to a first session, and there should not be — a single session is how a family actually finds out whether a tutor's style, pace and communication work for their child. Start with the subject inside the Career-related Programme that is causing the most immediate concern, whether that is the IGCSE content itself or the applied coursework running alongside it. Give the tutor real information upfront: what has been covered in school so far, whether a coursework deadline is already on the calendar, and which exam session the student is working toward. That context turns a first session from a generic introduction into a genuinely diagnostic one. From there, online, home or hybrid delivery is confirmed based on where a suitable tutor is actually available, not assumed in advance, and a written plan follows with checkpoints a parent can actually check. Nothing here is guaranteed in outcome, and any promise of a specific grade should be treated as a warning sign rather than reassurance. What is offered instead is a matching process built around the two things that actually determine whether CP tutoring works: whether the tutor has taught this exact combination before, and whether the schedule survives a real term. Both of those can be verified before any payment is made, and both are worth confirming before committing to anything longer than one session.
items: Start with the subject causing the most immediate concern
Share what's already been covered in school and any coursework deadline
Delivery mode confirmed based on actual tutor availability
A written plan with checkpoints follows the first session
No outcome is guaranteed — treat grade promises as a warning sign

faqs.question: How much does IGCSE Career-related Programme tutoring cost?
faqs.answer: Fees depend on the subject, the tutor's experience level, the exam board, and whether sessions are online, home or hybrid — home tutoring costs more once a tutor's travel time is factored in. There is no single published rate because CP combines an IGCSE subject with career-related coursework support, and pricing reflects that combined workload rather than a flat per-hour figure. The honest answer is to ask for a quote against your child's subject and schedule rather than trusting an advertised range, since two families with the same subject label can still get different quotes depending on grade band and frequency.

faqs.question: Which exam session should we target, May/June or October/November?
faqs.answer: That depends on your child's school and which series it enters candidates for — Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel both run a May/June and an October/November session, and schools choose based on their own academic calendar and cohort. If your school has already confirmed the sitting, tutoring plans backward from that date for both the IGCSE subject content and the career-related coursework deadlines, which usually fall earlier. If it has not been confirmed yet, that is worth clarifying with the school before locking a tutoring schedule, because targeting the wrong series wastes time nobody gets back.

faqs.question: Is home tutoring available in cities like Delhi, Bangalore or Chennai for this programme?
faqs.answer: It can be, depending on whether a tutor with the right subject and exam-board experience happens to be based close enough to travel reasonably for that specific student. IB Gram receives regular requests for CP support from cities including Delhi, Bangalore, Chennai, Ghaziabad, Faridabad and several others, but home availability is confirmed case by case rather than promised upfront, because tutors who both teach this exact combination and live nearby are a smaller pool than online specialists. Where a home match is not practical, online or hybrid tutoring is usually the better real option rather than a compromise.

faqs.question: What happens if the tutor and my child just don't click?
faqs.answer: That gets raised with the coordinating team rather than left to fix itself, and a replacement tutor is arranged without the family starting the matching process from zero — the subject, grade and schedule information already on file carries over. A mismatch is not rare and it is not treated as a failure on the family's part; teaching style, pace and even accent or communication habits can matter more than subject expertise for some students, especially younger ones. The sooner it is flagged, the less time is lost.

faqs.question: Can online tutoring really deliver the same result as in-person for something as involved as CP?
faqs.answer: For the subject content, yes — screen-sharing past papers, live annotation and recorded sessions for review cover the same ground as an in-person lesson, and many students find replaying a recording afterward genuinely useful. Where online is genuinely weaker is with a student who needs physical presence to stay focused for a full hour, or with coursework that benefits from a tutor watching handwriting or lab technique directly. For most CP subject combinations, online works fine; for a small number of students, particularly younger ones or those with attention difficulties, home or hybrid is the more honest recommendation.

faqs.question: How do you check a tutor actually knows the Career-related Programme and not just the IGCSE subject on its own?
faqs.answer: By asking directly, before shortlisting, what the applied and reflective components involve for this subject combination, and by checking their prior history for evidence they have supported that side before, not just the exam-board content. A tutor who can only talk about syllabus topics and has nothing to say about coursework structure or internal deadlines is flagged during matching rather than presented to a family as CP-ready. This is one area where a generic 'IGCSE tutor' label is genuinely misleading, and it is worth a parent asking the same question directly on a first call, in their own words.

faqs.question: What if my child starts CP tutoring late, close to the exam session?
faqs.answer: It limits what is realistically achievable, and an honest tutor will say so rather than promising a full turnaround in a few weeks. Late starts still help — targeted past-paper practice and mark-scheme technique can lift a script noticeably even in a short window — but a coursework component that is significantly behind cannot always be recovered if a school's internal deadline has already passed. The right move is to be specific about what is actually still open: which papers, which coursework pieces, how many weeks remain before the school's own cutoff, not the exam board's.

faqs.question: Do you work with students who are behind in one subject but fine in the career-related coursework, or the other way round?
faqs.answer: Yes, and that split is common — a student can be comfortable with the applied, project-based side of CP and still struggle with the more traditional IGCSE subject content, or the reverse, where subject knowledge is solid but the reflective and coursework writing lags. Matching accounts for this directly rather than assuming a single tutor profile fits both needs equally; some families end up with more session time weighted toward whichever side is weaker. Tell the tutor which side is stronger at the outset so time is not spent re-teaching what your child already has covered.

faqs.question: Is there a minimum commitment, or can we book a single session first?
faqs.answer: A single session first is genuinely fine, and it is the recommended way to start for exactly this reason — CP tutoring is a big enough combination of moving parts that a family should confirm fit before committing to a term-length plan. If it works, sessions typically settle into a weekly rhythm because that is what actually produces progress against a syllabus and a coursework deadline; sporadic, occasional sessions rarely do. If it does not work after that first session, there is no obligation to continue.

h1: IGCSE Diploma Programme Tutors for Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel Learners
heroTitle: IGCSE Diploma Programme Tutoring, Wherever You Are
heroSubtitle: A tutor who knows the Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel syllabus, works to the mark scheme, and turns up for the May/June or October/November session prepared. Sessions run online in your family's own time zone, with home tutoring where a tutor is genuinely local.
introSummary: Looking for IGCSE Diploma Programme tutors usually means one of two things: a subject grade has slipped, or exams are close enough that a plan is overdue. Either way, the fix is the same — a tutor who works to the actual Cambridge or Pearson Edexcel syllabus and mark scheme, not a generic revision guide. IB Gram matches families to subject specialists for online sessions in their own time zone, or home tutoring where a tutor happens to be local. Matching depends on subject, level and tutor availability at the time you enquire, not a guaranteed instant fit.

contentBlocks.heading: What Changes Between September and the Exam Session
contentBlocks.body: A family usually starts looking for IGCSE Diploma Programme tutors after a report card, not before one. That's fine — most support here begins reactively, and there is nothing wrong with correcting course mid-year rather than pretending a plan existed from day one. What matters more is what the next few months are meant to produce. At the start, a tutor should be able to say, specifically, which paper or unit is weak and why, based on actual working shown, not a general sense that science is hard. Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel publish assessment objectives for a reason: they tell you exactly what a mark scheme is rewarding, and a tutor who ignores that is teaching the subject, not the exam. Age bands and entry points vary by subject and level, so the right starting point for a fifteen-year-old sitting Physics in November looks nothing like the plan for a student two years out. By the middle of the year, the work should have shifted from explanation to retrieval — past papers done under rough time pressure, errors logged by type, not just marked right or wrong. By the final stretch before the May/June or October/November series, the tutor's job is narrower: pacing, paper-specific habits, and calm. If a student is still being taught new content two weeks before the exam, something was left too late, and that is worth saying plainly rather than dressing up as extra revision.
items: Early term: pinpoint the actual weak paper, not the whole subject
Mid-year: shift from explanation to timed past-paper practice
Final weeks: pacing, command-word habits, exam-day routine
A late start narrows what's realistically achievable before the session

contentBlocks.heading: Online, Home, or Both — Matching the Mode to the Situation
contentBlocks.body: Online tutoring gives access to a specialist in a subject a family might not find within a reasonable travel radius at all — an Additional Maths tutor, say, or someone who has actually marked Economics Paper 2 scripts. It runs in the family's own time zone, which matters more than it sounds once you're coordinating a working parent's evening and a student's school day on two different clocks. Home tutoring, by contrast, suits younger learners who focus better with someone physically in the room, and it depends entirely on a tutor's willingness and ability to travel that route — it is not available everywhere a family might want it, and pretending otherwise wastes everyone's time. A hybrid arrangement — weekly online sessions plus an occasional in-person block before a mock or a real exam — is common for older students who want the flexibility of online but a bit of in-person accountability closer to test dates. None of these is universally better. A twelve-year-old who drifts on video calls may do genuinely better work at a kitchen table with someone present. A seventeen-year-old juggling five subjects usually gets more from online, simply because it removes travel time from an already tight week. The honest answer to which mode to pick is: whichever one the student will actually show up to consistently, twice a week, for three months.
items: Online: specialist access regardless of city, in your own time zone
Home: better focus for younger students, subject to tutor travel range
Hybrid: weekly online plus in-person sessions before mocks or exams
The right mode is the one attended consistently, not the fanciest one

contentBlocks.heading: Where Subject Depth Actually Shows Up
contentBlocks.body: IGCSE Diploma Programme tutors are only as useful as their depth in the specific subject and board, and depth looks different by subject. In Mathematics and Additional Maths, it shows up in a tutor's ability to spot which technique a student defaults to under pressure and correct it before the exam, not just walk through worked examples. In the sciences — Physics, Chemistry, Biology — it shows up in practical-based questions and data-handling, an area many students lose marks on quietly because the content feels secondary to the real theory. In English Language and Literature, it's less about content and more about training a student to answer the actual question asked, which sounds obvious and is routinely not done. Business Studies and Economics reward students who can apply a concept to an unfamiliar case study rather than recite a definition, and a tutor who only drills definitions is preparing a student for a different, easier exam than the one they'll sit. Second-language subjects and Humanities options each carry their own command-word conventions that differ from board to board. None of this is a case for hiring the most expensive tutor available. It is a case for being specific when asking what a prospective tutor has actually taught before, and for how long, in exactly this subject and board combination — not IGCSE tutoring as a blanket category.
items: Maths/Additional Maths: technique correction under exam pressure
Sciences: practical and data-handling questions, often the quiet mark-losers
English: answering the question asked, not writing a generic essay
Business/Economics: applying concepts to case studies, not reciting definitions

contentBlocks.heading: Where Home Sessions Can Reach, and Where Online Fills the Gap
contentBlocks.body: Home tutoring for the IGCSE Diploma Programme already reaches families in cities as varied as Ahmedabad, Bangalore, Bhopal, Bhubaneswar, Chandigarh, Chennai, Coimbatore, Dehradun, Delhi, Faridabad, Ghaziabad and Greater Noida — and plenty of others besides, since availability is really a question of which tutors happen to live and travel within reach of a given family, not a fixed service map. That is the honest constraint of home tutoring anywhere: it depends on a specific tutor's route, not on IB Gram's coverage in the abstract. A family in a city with strong tutor density might get three suitable in-person options; a family somewhere quieter might get none, and that's not a failure of the platform, it's geography. Online tutoring exists precisely to remove that constraint. A student anywhere, in any of these cities or well beyond them, can work with a subject specialist without either party traveling, and the session happens at a time that suits the family's own clock rather than a tutor's commute. The trade-off is real, though: online loses the in-person cues a home tutor picks up on automatically — a student's body language when they're lost, the ability to physically point at a diagram. For some students that loss doesn't matter. For a student who is anxious, distractible, or new to independent study, it can matter quite a bit, and a hybrid plan is often the better answer than picking one mode and hoping.
items: Home tutoring depends on a specific tutor's travel route, not a fixed map
Cities with more tutors nearby naturally have more home options
Online removes the geography question entirely, worldwide
Hybrid plans exist because online genuinely loses in-person cues

contentBlocks.heading: Where This Fits Next to GCSE, A Level and the IB Diploma
contentBlocks.body: IGCSE sits ahead of most other pre-university programmes chronologically, and a family's later choices are shaped more by this stage than they usually realise at the time. A student aiming for A Levels afterwards benefits from an IGCSE tutor who teaches slightly beyond the syllabus minimum in subjects likely to be continued, because the jump in difficulty at the next stage is real and rarely gently sloped. A student heading toward the IB Diploma Programme instead faces a different shift — from single-subject depth toward the breadth of six subjects plus the Extended Essay, Theory of Knowledge and CAS, and an IGCSE tutor who understands that shift can frame the current subject as preparation for managing several demanding subjects simultaneously, not just for passing one exam. Coursework-heavy subjects are worth flagging early regardless of the destination programme, since coursework and internal-assessment habits — planning, drafting, meeting interim deadlines — transfer directly into IA and Extended Essay work later, and a student who never learned to self-pace a piece of coursework at fourteen often struggles more with an IA at sixteen than the subject content would predict. None of this means over-planning three years ahead for a twelve-year-old. It means the tutor working with a student now should at least know what comes next, even loosely, rather than treating each syllabus as a closed box.
items: IGCSE performance shapes what's realistic at A Level or IB Diploma
A Level-bound students benefit from slightly beyond-syllabus teaching now
IB Diploma-bound students need early practice managing several subjects at once
Coursework habits learned now carry into IA and Extended Essay work later

contentBlocks.heading: How a Family Actually Gets Paired With a Tutor
contentBlocks.body: The process starts with specifics, not a subject name. A parent describes the exam board if known, the current grade or predicted level, the exact syllabus component causing trouble if one has been identified, and roughly how many sessions a week the family can realistically sustain — not aspirationally, realistically, because a plan for three sessions a week that collapses to one after a fortnight helps nobody. From there, tutors are shortlisted against subject, board and level rather than general availability, and a parent typically sees more than one option so the choice isn't take-it-or-leave-it. A short introductory conversation, sometimes with the student present, usually settles whether the tutor's style and the student's temperament are a reasonable fit — a fast-talking, banter-heavy tutor might be exactly right for one student and wrong for another who needs more patience and less energy. First-session content is agreed in advance: usually a short diagnostic exercise plus a look at recent schoolwork, so the tutor isn't starting cold and the first hour isn't wasted on introductions. None of this guarantees an instant match on the first try. Subject-and-board combinations that are less common take longer to fill well, and a family should expect that honestly rather than being told everything is available immediately regardless of how niche the request is.
items: Start with board, level and the specific weak component, not just a subject name
Tutors are shortlisted by subject/board/level match, with more than one option shown
A short intro conversation checks style and temperament fit before committing
Rarer subject-board combinations genuinely take longer to fill well

contentBlocks.heading: What Gets Checked Before Anyone Is Introduced
contentBlocks.body: Every tutor on the platform is reviewed for subject qualification and relevant teaching or tutoring experience before being matched to a family, and that check is specific to the subject and board being requested rather than a blanket qualified-to-tutor tick. A tutor who has taught Cambridge Biology for years isn't automatically vetted for Pearson Edexcel Additional Maths — the two are checked separately because the syllabuses, command words and mark schemes genuinely differ. Exam-board familiarity is asked about directly: has this tutor actually studied recent past papers and examiner reports for this specification, or only taught IGCSE-level content in general terms. Background and identity checks are part of onboarding, and a parent is welcome to ask what was verified for a specific tutor rather than taking it on faith. None of this is a guarantee of outcome — a well-qualified tutor and a distracted, unmotivated student can still produce a flat term, and it would be dishonest to promise otherwise. What the vetting actually buys a family is a reasonable floor: a tutor who knows the subject and the exam, not someone learning the syllabus alongside the student. If a match isn't working after a fair trial, that's a scheduling and personality-fit conversation, not evidence the vetting failed.
items: Qualification and experience checked per subject and exam board, not generically
Exam-board familiarity is asked about directly, not assumed
Identity and background checks happen at onboarding, and details can be asked about
Vetting sets a floor on competence; it can't guarantee student motivation

contentBlocks.heading: Which School Types This Suits, Stated Without Overclaiming
contentBlocks.body: IGCSE Diploma Programme tutoring is used by students at British-curriculum schools, international schools offering Cambridge or Pearson Edexcel syllabuses, and occasionally by students moving between curricula mid-way through secondary school who need to catch up on syllabus content covered differently elsewhere. The common thread isn't the school's name or reputation — it's whether the student's day-to-day class time is keeping pace with the syllabus, and whether the gap, if there is one, is content-based or exam-technique-based, because those need different tutoring approaches entirely. It's worth being direct here: IB Gram is an independent tutoring platform and is not officially affiliated with the IB Organization, Cambridge International or Pearson Edexcel. No claim is made, implied or otherwise, of a school partnership, an examiner relationship, or insider access to unpublished material. What a tutor brings instead is familiarity with the publicly available syllabus documents, specimen papers, mark schemes and examiner reports — the same material a diligent student or parent could review directly, applied with more experience and more consistency than most families have time for on their own. A parent moving a child between school systems, or comparing a school's own internal report against actual past-paper performance, is exactly the kind of situation where an outside, syllabus-literate tutor earns their place rather than duplicating what the school already provides well.
items: Used across British-curriculum and international schools running Cambridge or Pearson Edexcel
Also used by students switching curricula mid-secondary school
No affiliation with the IB Organization, Cambridge International or Pearson Edexcel
Value comes from syllabus literacy and consistency, not insider access

contentBlocks.heading: What Four Weeks In Should Actually Show
contentBlocks.body: By roughly the fourth week, a parent should be able to point to something concrete, not just a general sense that sessions are going well. That might be a past-paper score that has moved, a specific type of question the student no longer panics over, or simply a student who has started doing the set homework unprompted instead of the week before an exam. If none of that is visible, it's worth a direct conversation rather than quietly continuing for another month hoping it self-corrects. Sometimes the issue is pace — the tutor moving faster or slower than the student needs. Sometimes it's personality, which is nobody's fault and doesn't need a drawn-out justification to fix; a tutor swap after a genuine trial is a normal part of getting this right, not an admission of failure by either side. Sometimes the real issue isn't the tutor at all but the schedule — a session squeezed in after a long school day and two other activities rarely goes well regardless of who is teaching it. A useful four-week check covers three things plainly: has a specific weak area actually narrowed, is the student engaging rather than being talked at, and is the session slot realistic given everything else in the week. Two out of three isn't a crisis. Zero out of three is a reason to change something now rather than at the next report card.
items: Look for a concrete change: a score, a question type, unprompted homework
A tutor swap after a fair trial is normal, not a failure
Check whether the real problem is pace, personality, or scheduling
Two out of three progress signs is fine; zero is a reason to act now

contentBlocks.heading: Starting Without Committing to a Year Upfront
contentBlocks.body: A sensible first step is smaller than most families assume it needs to be: one subject, a stated exam board if known, and a plan for four to six weeks rather than a full academic year signed up in advance. That's enough time to see whether the tutor's approach suits the student and whether the schedule actually survives contact with real life — sports practice, other homework, the odd week where everything gets cancelled. Session frequency should be set around what's sustainable, not what sounds thorough on paper; two focused sessions a week beat four that get skipped half the time. It's worth deciding in advance what working will look like at the four-week mark — a specific paper attempted under time, a topic the student stopped avoiding — so the review isn't just a vague gut check. If the exam session is close, that changes the calculus: near May/June or October/November, the priority shifts from broad coverage to the highest-value gaps, and a tutor should say so plainly rather than trying to cover the whole syllabus in six weeks because that's what was originally asked for. None of this requires a long call or a sales pitch. It requires naming the subject, the board if known, the current situation honestly, and letting the matching process do the rest, with the option to change course early if the first fit isn't the right one.
items: Start with one subject and a four-to-six-week trial, not a full year
Set a concrete definition of 'working' before the trial begins
Close to an exam session, prioritise the highest-value gaps over full coverage
Changing the plan or the tutor early is normal, not a setback

faqs.question: How much does an IGCSE Diploma Programme tutor cost?
faqs.answer: Fees vary by subject, tutor experience and session frequency, and are confirmed once a specific tutor is shortlisted rather than fixed in advance — a tutor experienced with Additional Maths or Physics at a senior level typically costs more than a general-subject tutor at an earlier stage. Online sessions are often more cost-effective than home tutoring simply because there's no travel time being paid for. The honest way to budget is to ask for a rate range at the shortlisting stage for the exact subject and board in question, rather than assuming one number applies across every subject IB Gram covers.

faqs.question: Does online tutoring actually work for exam preparation, or is in-person better?
faqs.answer: For most subjects and most students, yes — online tutoring works well for exam preparation because past papers, mark schemes and worked solutions can all be shared on screen just as clearly as on paper, and recordings can be revisited. It tends to work less well for younger students who need more physical presence to stay focused, or for subjects with heavy practical components where demonstrating something hands-on genuinely helps. If a student has struggled to concentrate on video calls before, that's worth flagging upfront so a hybrid or home arrangement is considered instead.

faqs.question: What happens if my child's grades don't improve after a few months?
faqs.answer: First, check whether progress is being measured concretely — a past-paper score, a specific error type reducing — rather than just a feeling that sessions are pleasant. If there's genuinely no movement after a fair trial with reasonable session frequency, the usual next steps are a tutor change, a change in session frequency, or a harder look at whether something outside tutoring, such as motivation or an undiagnosed gap from an earlier year, is the actual blocker. Tutoring can't fix a problem it was never told about.

faqs.question: Can we change tutors if the first one isn't a good fit?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it's a normal part of getting the match right rather than something to feel awkward about. A short trial period is the right time to notice whether the pace, personality or teaching style suits the student, and raising it early is easier for everyone than persisting for a term out of politeness. A replacement tutor is shortlisted the same way the first one was, against subject, board and level, and usually the second attempt benefits from what the family learned about what didn't work the first time.

faqs.question: Is home tutoring available everywhere, or only in certain cities?
faqs.answer: It depends on tutor availability in a given area rather than a fixed list of covered cities — home tutoring exists where a suitable tutor happens to live and is willing to travel, which naturally varies. Cities with more tutors registered tend to have more home options; quieter areas may have few or none for a specific subject-board combination. Online tutoring is the reliable fallback everywhere, since it removes the travel constraint entirely, and many families end up choosing it by default even where home tutoring is technically available, simply for the added flexibility.

faqs.question: What exam boards does this cover, and does it matter which one my child is on?
faqs.answer: Tutoring is organised around the published Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel syllabuses, and yes, the board matters more than parents often expect — the two set different assessment objectives, command words and, in several subjects, meaningfully different content emphasis. A tutor experienced with one board isn't automatically fluent in the other's mark scheme conventions. Confirming the exact board and syllabus code when requesting a tutor, rather than just naming the subject, makes the shortlisting faster and the eventual match more useful from the first session.

faqs.question: How soon before the May/June or October/November exam session should tutoring start?
faqs.answer: Earlier is better, but starting late isn't pointless, it's just narrower in what it can achieve. Six months out, there's time to close content gaps and build real technique. Six weeks out, the honest priority becomes triaging the highest-value gaps and exam-day habits rather than attempting full syllabus coverage, and a tutor should say that plainly rather than promising a full turnaround that isn't realistic in the time left. Starting the week before the exam mostly helps with nerves and last-minute technique, not content.

faqs.question: My child is moving from a different school system mid-year — can a tutor help them catch up?
faqs.answer: Yes, this is a fairly common situation, and it usually needs a slightly different approach than routine tutoring: a quick audit of which syllabus content has already been covered in the previous system versus what Cambridge or Pearson Edexcel expects at this stage, followed by a focused plan to close whichever gaps show up, rather than repeating everything from scratch. Timing matters — the closer this happens to an exam session, the more selective the catch-up plan needs to be about what actually gets covered.

faqs.question: How many sessions a week does a student actually need?
faqs.answer: It depends on the size of the gap and how close the exam session is, not a fixed rule. One focused session a week is often enough for a student who's broadly on track and just wants steady reinforcement. Two or more becomes reasonable when a specific paper is genuinely weak or the exam session is close. More sessions than a student can realistically sustain alongside school and other commitments tends to backfire — skipped or half-attended sessions teach less than fewer, fully-present ones, regardless of how thorough the schedule looks on paper.

faqs.question: Do tutors help with coursework or internal assessment, not just exam papers?
faqs.answer: Where a subject includes coursework, a tutor can help with planning, drafting and meeting interim deadlines, though the final work has to be the student's own — that's a requirement of the boards themselves, not a platform policy. What a tutor can usefully do is review structure, flag where a mark scheme's criteria aren't being addressed clearly, and help a student pace multi-stage coursework so it isn't rushed in the final week, which is where a lot of otherwise-capable students lose marks unnecessarily.
