faqs.question: What exactly is the IB Career-related Programme, and how is tutoring for it different from Diploma Programme tutoring?
faqs.answer: The Career-related Programme pairs two or three Diploma Programme courses with a career-related study and a four-part core: Personal and Professional Skills, Service Learning, Language Development and the Reflective Project. DP tutoring on its own only covers half of that. A CP tutor needs to teach the specific DP courses a student has chosen to the same standard as any DP tutor, but also understand how the core components are assessed against published criteria rather than examined in a single sitting. The two aren't interchangeable roles, which is why matching asks specifically about CP rather than treating it as a smaller DP.

faqs.question: What does tutoring for the Career-related Programme typically cost?
faqs.answer: Fees depend on the DP course and level being taught, whether sessions are online, home or hybrid, and how experienced the matched tutor is. There's no single rate that applies across every subject or country. Online tutoring is generally the most flexible on cost since there's no travel involved. Home tutoring in a given city reflects local availability and tends to cost more where qualified tutors for a specific course are scarce. Exact pricing is discussed and agreed before a single session is booked, not adjusted afterward, and a family can ask for the fee structure upfront without it affecting matching.

faqs.question: Can a tutor actually help with the Reflective Project without it becoming an academic honesty problem?
faqs.answer: Yes, within clear limits. A tutor can help a student choose and narrow an ethical issue, structure the argument, understand the assessment criteria, and give feedback on drafts, the same kind of supervision a school would expect from a mentor. What a tutor should not do is write or substantially rewrite content, because the Reflective Project is meant to be independent, supervised work, and it is treated as seriously as the Extended Essay on this point. A tutor who offers to write it for you is not one worth working with, whatever the price.

faqs.question: Does online tutoring really work for a programme that includes practical components like Service Learning?
faqs.answer: For the academic DP courses, yes. A specialist online is often a better fit than a generalist nearby, since not every local tutor teaches every DP course at every level. For Service Learning specifically, online tutoring can help with reflection, logging and structuring the write-up, but it can't substitute for the actual service activity, which happens in the student's own community regardless of how tutoring is arranged. Personal and Professional Skills sits in between: some of it works fine over a call, and some students genuinely do better with someone in the room. Hybrid exists for exactly that mix.

faqs.question: What happens if the first tutor isn't the right fit?
faqs.answer: Switching is a normal, unremarkable part of the process, not something that needs a long justification. Fit issues usually show up within the first couple of sessions: pacing that's wrong for the student, a teaching style that doesn't land, or a tutor who turns out to know the subject less deeply at that specific level than the match suggested. Flagging it early is more useful than waiting it out for a term, since CP timelines, Reflective Project deadlines, mock exams, Service Learning check-ins, don't pause while a mismatch gets resolved. A replacement is arranged from the same shortlist process as the original match.

faqs.question: Our child is only taking two DP courses under CP instead of six. Does that make tutoring simpler?
faqs.answer: In some ways, yes: there's less to schedule and coordinate. But it doesn't make the tutoring itself lighter, because the two or three courses chosen under CP are examined to the same standard, at the same level, as they would be for a full DP student. What changes is that a CP student also carries the four core components alongside those courses, which a full DP student doesn't have in the same form. So the academic tutoring load per course is identical; the difference is the additional, non-examined work sitting around it, which needs its own attention rather than being assumed to look after itself.

faqs.question: How does tutoring change around the May and November exam sessions?
faqs.answer: Internal assessment and coursework deadlines are set by each school individually, so the run-up looks different depending on which session a student is sitting and what their school's internal calendar requires. In the months before an exam session, tutoring typically shifts toward past-paper practice, mark-scheme technique and mock preparation for the specific DP courses chosen. Outside that window, there's more room for foundational work on weaker topics and steady progress on the Reflective Project and Service Learning logging, which are easier to manage well ahead of a deadline than compressed into the final weeks before it.

faqs.question: Is IB Gram affiliated with the IB Organization or with the schools it mentions?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram is an independent tutoring platform. It is not officially affiliated with the IB Organization, Cambridge International or Pearson Edexcel, and it does not set curriculum, run examinations or issue grades. What it does is match families with tutors who are experienced in the specific courses and assessment criteria a student is working with. Any reference to IB programmes, courses or assessment components on this page describes publicly available curriculum structure, not an endorsement from or partnership with the IB Organization itself.

faqs.question: What if there's no real progress after a few weeks of tutoring?
faqs.answer: The four-week point is a reasonable place to check honestly rather than hope it improves on its own. If a student still can't explain what they've covered, or a specific weakness identified in the first session hasn't moved, that's worth raising rather than continuing quietly. Sometimes the fix is a different tutor; sometimes it's a different approach with the same tutor, more diagnostic and less content-heavy; and occasionally the honest answer is that the timeline is unrealistic given how close a deadline already is. None of these is a guaranteed fix, but naming the problem early leaves more options than naming it late.

faqs.question: We're in Bangalore. Can we get a home tutor for CP, or does it have to be online?
faqs.answer: Home tutoring in Bangalore, like in the other cities currently covered, depends on whether a tutor qualified in the specific DP courses your child needs happens to be within reasonable travel, and that can vary month to month. Where the right subject match isn't available locally, the more reliable option is a specialist online for the DP courses, paired with a local tutor for the Personal and Professional Skills side if that's where the actual need is. That hybrid arrangement is often more realistic in a large, traffic-heavy city than insisting on one home tutor who covers everything.

faqs.question: Can one tutor cover both a DP course and the CP core components, or do we need two different tutors?
faqs.answer: Occasionally one tutor can do both, if they have both the subject qualification and genuine experience with Reflective Project supervision or Service Learning reflection, but it's uncommon and shouldn't be assumed. More often it works better as two separate matches: a subject specialist for the DP course, and a tutor experienced specifically in CP's core, since coaching independent research and structuring reflection are distinct skills from teaching syllabus content. Asking for both roles from one person, unless they're genuinely qualified for both, tends to produce weaker results in each.

heroTitle: IB Diploma Programme Tutoring, Built Around Your Timetable
heroSubtitle: A DP timetable rarely leaves room for a fixed evening slot. IB Gram matches your family with a subject-specific tutor for HL and SL courses, TOK, EE and CAS planning, working in your own time zone, whether you need one subject shored up or a full six-subject support plan.
introSummary: It's 9pm, the DP student still has an IA draft due Friday and a maths problem set unfinished, and the family is trying to figure out whether a tutor can even fit into this week. IB Diploma Programme tutors on IB Gram are matched by subject and level — HL Physics is not the same search as SL Physics — and lessons run online worldwide in the family's own time zone, with home and hybrid tutoring where a tutor happens to be local. Matching depends on subject, level and the tutor's current availability, not a guarantee of instant access.

contentBlocks.heading: What a DP Tutor Actually Spends Time On
contentBlocks.body: Diploma Programme study runs across two years, usually for students aged sixteen to nineteen, and it asks for six subjects at Higher or Standard Level plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. A tutor working inside this structure is not simply reteaching a topic from a textbook. IB assessment is criterion-related, which means a Physics HL paper and a Physics SL paper are marked against different descriptors, and an English essay is graded on command terms — 'evaluate', 'discuss', 'to what extent' — that carry specific expectations most school revision guides skip past. IB Gram matches families to tutors who work inside that structure deliberately: subject and level first, then the internal assessment or coursework component that is actually due, then the exam session the student is sitting. May and November are the two IB examination sessions, and each school sets its own internal deadlines for IAs and mock exams ahead of them, so a useful tutor plans backward from the school's calendar, not a generic one. Academic honesty is treated seriously throughout — an IA draft is coached, not written, and any tutor who blurs that line is doing the student a disservice that surfaces at the worst possible time, during moderation. None of this is exotic. It is the ordinary, slightly tedious discipline of matching subject depth to what the syllabus and mark scheme actually reward, session after session, until the pattern holds under exam pressure.

contentBlocks.heading: Where Families Are Logging In From
contentBlocks.body: A DP family in one time zone and a tutor in another is now the normal case, not the exception. IB Gram runs online sessions in the family's own time zone rather than the tutor's, which matters more than it sounds: a 7pm slot reads very differently depending on where the family actually is, and scheduling is built around the student's evening, not a fixed shift. Because DP is offered by schools worldwide, the platform is not built around one country's timetable or one region's exam patterns — students preparing for May or November sessions are matched the same way regardless of where their school sits. Home tutoring is different: it depends entirely on a tutor already being local to the student, which is why it is offered subject to availability rather than promised upfront. Among the hub cities where IB Gram has seen tutor coverage build up are Ahmedabad, Bangalore, Bhopal, Bhubaneswar, Chandigarh, Chennai, Coimbatore, Dehradun, Delhi, Faridabad, Ghaziabad and Greater Noida — useful as examples of how coverage clusters around cities with several IB schools nearby, not as a complete list of where a tutor can be found. A family outside any of these does not lose access to a tutor; it simply means the realistic option is online or, if a tutor genuinely happens to be nearby, a hybrid plan that mixes both.

Same matching process regardless of the school's country
Home tutoring depends on a tutor already being local
Coverage clusters around cities with several IB schools nearby

contentBlocks.heading: Online, Home or Something in Between
contentBlocks.body: None of the three modes is automatically the right one. Online tutoring is the only way to reach a subject specialist regardless of where the family lives — a school offering an unusual Group 6 arts subject, or Further Mathematics HL, often cannot be matched to a local home tutor at all, because the pool of people teaching that specific course in that city may be very small. Screen-sharing a mark scheme, working through past-paper questions live and annotating a draft IA in real time cover most of what a DP subject actually needs. Home tutoring suits a different situation: a younger student who loses focus without someone physically present, or a family that wants a fixed weekly rhythm in the house rather than a login. It is also the mode most limited by geography — a tutor has to be willing and able to travel, which narrows the realistic pool sharply compared to online, and it is simply not available everywhere. Hybrid plans try to take the better half of each: a subject specialist online for the harder HL content, with a local tutor or the same tutor visiting occasionally for exam-season intensity. The honest trade-off is this — hybrid costs more coordination, not necessarily more money by itself, because two schedules now have to align instead of one. Families choosing between the three usually get furthest by naming the actual problem first — a weak subject, a motivation problem, a scheduling clash — rather than picking a mode and hoping it fits.

Home suits younger students needing someone physically present
Home tutoring is the most geography-limited of the three
Hybrid mixes a specialist online with occasional in-person sessions
Hybrid needs more schedule coordination, not necessarily more spend

contentBlocks.heading: Six Subject Groups, One HL/SL Decision Each
contentBlocks.body: The Diploma Programme's structure is the same everywhere: six subject groups, typically three studied at Higher Level and three at Standard Level, plus the Extended Essay, Theory of Knowledge and CAS running underneath all six. That structure sounds simple until a family tries to tutor for it. HL and SL of the same subject share a name but not a syllabus depth — HL Chemistry works through material and problem types that SL Chemistry does not touch, so a tutor who taught the SL course last year is not automatically ready for an HL student this year, and it is worth asking directly which level a prospective tutor has actually taught. The Extended Essay sits outside any one subject group and needs a supervisor-style relationship more than a lesson — regular short check-ins on argument and sourcing, not a weekly hour of content delivery. Theory of Knowledge is different again: it rewards a student who can hold two subjects' worth of knowledge claims in tension, which is a skill some excellent subject teachers are not equipped to coach. CAS is not tutored in the conventional sense at all, but a tutor who understands its reflection requirements can stop a student from treating it as an afterthought in the final term, when reflections are hardest to reconstruct honestly. A tutor search should start from the specific subject and level, move to whether EE or TOK support is also needed, and only then consider scheduling — reversing that order usually wastes the first few sessions.
items: Six subject groups, HL/SL combinations set by the school
HL and SL share a name but not a syllabus depth
EE support works better as regular check-ins than weekly lessons
TOK needs cross-subject thinking, not single-subject expertise
CAS reflection is easiest to do well before the final term

contentBlocks.heading: How a Tutor Actually Gets Matched
contentBlocks.body: The matching itself is deliberately unglamorous. A family describes the subject, the level, the school's syllabus variant if it has one, and the actual problem — a weak IA draft, a slipping predicted grade, a student who has fallen behind after missing school. IB Gram uses that description to filter for tutors who have taught that specific subject at that specific level recently, not simply 'IB experience' as a vague label, because a tutor who taught IB Biology SL five years ago is a different match than one teaching HL Biology this term. Subject-level fit is checked before anything else, availability second, and price fit last — reversing that order is how families end up with a tutor who is available and affordable but wrong for the subject. A short first conversation, usually direct with the tutor, is where fit gets tested for real: does the tutor ask about the school's specific IA topic, or the exact command terms the last paper used, before quoting a plan. A tutor who talks in generalities about 'IB support' rather than the syllabus in front of them is a signal worth noticing early, not after four paid sessions. If the first match is not right, IB Gram treats that as normal rather than a failure — a subject mismatch or a personality mismatch is more common than families expect, and swapping tutors after an honest first attempt costs far less than persisting with a poor fit through an entire exam session.
items: Subject and level filtered first, then availability, then price
Recent teaching experience at that exact level, not general IB history
A short first conversation tests fit before committing to a plan
Tutor swaps are normal, not a sign the process failed
Watch for vague 'IB support' language instead of syllabus specifics

contentBlocks.heading: Where DP Fits in the Wider IB Continuum
contentBlocks.body: DP is the last of four IB programmes, arriving after the Primary Years Programme and Middle Years Programme, and it is built for students roughly sixteen to nineteen, in the last two years before university. Some schools also offer the IB Career-related Programme alongside DP, which shares TOK and CAS elements but pairs subjects with a career-related study rather than a sixth academic subject — a distinction worth checking if a family is unsure which programme their child is actually enrolled in. A student can register as a full Diploma candidate, sitting all six subjects plus the core, or as a Course candidate, taking individual DP subjects without the full diploma award — and a tutor plan should differ depending on which applies, since a Course candidate does not need EE or TOK support at all. The two-year span means timing matters more than it looks: a tutor engaged in the first term of year one has time to build subject depth before IA deadlines start landing in year two, while a family that starts tutoring six months before the May or November exam session is working with a narrower set of realistic goals — closing specific gaps rather than rebuilding a subject from the ground up. That is not a reason to delay starting if the need is already visible; it is a reason to be precise about what tutoring at that stage can and cannot fix.

CP shares TOK and CAS with DP but swaps a subject for career study
Diploma candidates sit all six subjects plus the core; Course candidates do not
Year one is for building depth; year two is deadline-driven
Starting close to an exam session narrows realistic goals, honestly

contentBlocks.heading: Working Around Your School's Own Calendar, Not Instead of It
contentBlocks.body: IB Gram is an independent tutoring platform and is not affiliated with the IB Organization, Cambridge International or Pearson Edexcel, and it has no relationship with any particular school. That independence is deliberate rather than a limitation: it means a tutor's first job is to work around the school's own IA deadlines, mock exam dates and coursework schedule, not to replace or contradict what the school's IB coordinator has already set. A good tutor asks early for whatever the school has already given the student — the IA rubric with the coordinator's comments, the mock exam paper, the predicted grade and the reasoning behind it — because tutoring that ignores this and starts from a generic syllabus outline wastes the most useful information already sitting in the student's inbox. Where a coordinator has flagged a specific weakness — poor exam technique under time pressure, thin exemplification in essay-based subjects, weak referencing in the EE — that flag should shape the first month of tutoring directly rather than getting rediscovered from scratch. This coordination matters more in DP than in earlier programmes because criterion-related assessment means the school's own feedback, tied to specific mark bands, is more precise than a generic 'weak in maths' summary would be. Families sometimes hesitate to share school feedback with an outside tutor; in practice, withholding it usually just means paying for the tutor to re-diagnose something the school already diagnosed for free.
items: Independent platform, no affiliation with IB, Cambridge or Pearson Edexcel
Tutors work from existing IA feedback and mock results, not a blank slate
School-flagged weaknesses should shape the first month directly
Coordinator comments are usually more precise than a general subject label
Sharing school feedback with a tutor saves paying to rediscover it

contentBlocks.heading: What Actually Gets Checked Before a Tutor Is Listed
contentBlocks.body: Vetting is about verifiable specifics, not a badge or a star rating. IB Gram checks a tutor's stated qualifications and subject background before listing them, and separately checks which subjects and levels they claim direct teaching or tutoring experience in, because those are two different things — a subject degree does not automatically mean recent HL teaching experience, and the two get checked separately rather than assumed from each other. Exam-board familiarity is checked in a similar way: has the tutor actually marked, moderated or closely reviewed IB-style mark schemes recently, or is their familiarity from several years ago, before a command-term emphasis or a syllabus shifted. None of this produces a guaranteed outcome, and IB Gram does not claim one — no tutor, however well matched, can promise a particular grade or a numeric improvement, and any platform claiming otherwise is not being straight with families. What verification does produce is a narrower, more honest starting point: a family knows roughly what a tutor has actually taught before the first paid session, rather than finding out in week three that the tutor's HL experience was really SL experience under a different name. A parent is entitled to ask directly which levels a tutor has taught in the last two years, and a tutor who cannot answer specifically is worth treating with more caution than one who can.
items: Qualifications and subject background checked before listing
Teaching experience checked separately, by exact subject and level
Recency of exam-board familiarity matters as much as its existence
No guaranteed grades or score claims, from IB Gram or any tutor
Parents can and should ask which levels a tutor taught recently

contentBlocks.heading: What the First Month Should Actually Show
contentBlocks.body: A first session with a DP tutor should produce something concrete before it ends — a short diagnostic on the actual syllabus content, not a generic getting-to-know-you hour, and a written note on what the next few weeks will focus on. By the end of week four, a parent should be able to point to something specific: a completed IA section that has moved from a first attempt to something closer to the mark scheme's language, a set of past-paper questions the student can now do without help that were previously a struggle, or at minimum a clearer, more honest picture of where the student actually stands relative to the target grade. If none of that is visible by week four, that is worth raising directly with the tutor rather than assuming it will resolve itself — a plan that is not producing visible movement after a month rarely fixes itself in month two without a change. IB Gram supports switching tutors when the fit is not working, and a family should not feel it is wasting sunk time by doing so; a mismatch caught early costs a handful of sessions, while one carried through to April of the exam year costs the exam attempt itself. One honest limitation is worth stating plainly: tutoring can close a knowledge or technique gap, and it can improve exam performance meaningfully, but it cannot substitute for a student's own classroom attendance and coursework engagement across the two years — no external tutor sees enough of the day-to-day school context to replace that.

Week four should show a specific, checkable improvement
No visible movement by week four is a signal to raise, not ignore
Switching tutors early costs far less than persisting with a poor fit
Tutoring cannot substitute for classroom attendance and coursework engagement

contentBlocks.heading: Starting This Week, Practically
contentBlocks.body: Starting does not require a long form or a lengthy call. A family names the subject, the level, the school's exam session — May or November — and the actual problem, whether that is a specific IA section, a slipping predicted grade, or exam technique that is not holding up under time pressure. IB Gram uses that to propose tutors who have taught that subject at that level recently, and a short first conversation, usually direct with the tutor, is where the family checks fit before committing to anything beyond a single session. It helps to have the school's own materials ready before that first session — the IA rubric with any coordinator comments, the most recent mock paper, the current predicted grade — because a tutor who starts from those instead of a blank syllabus outline gets to something useful faster. Pricing and session frequency are set between the family and the tutor directly and vary by subject, level and how much support is needed, so it is worth asking for a plan in writing rather than a single quoted rate. None of this needs to happen months in advance. A family six weeks from a mock exam with a specific weak topic is a normal starting point, not a late one, provided the goal for that window is realistic — closing one identified gap, not restructuring two years of study in six weeks. The first useful step is simply naming the subject, the level and the actual problem, in that order.

Have IA feedback, mock papers and predicted grade ready for session one
Pricing and frequency are agreed directly with the matched tutor

faqs.question: How is DP tutoring different from IGCSE or MYP tutoring?
faqs.answer: DP tutoring is built around criterion-related assessment, command terms and the IA/EE/TOK/CAS structure unique to the Diploma Programme, so it differs from IGCSE tutoring, which is exam-board content revision, and from MYP tutoring, which is broader and less exam-specific. A DP tutor should be comfortable with HL versus SL syllabus depth and with mark-scheme language for the exact subject, not just general IB familiarity. If your child is moving from MYP into DP, mention that during matching — the transition itself, particularly the jump in independent workload, is often the actual issue rather than any single subject.

faqs.question: Can a tutor actually help with the Extended Essay without writing it?
faqs.answer: No tutor should write or substantially redraft an Extended Essay — that breaches academic honesty rules and risks the essay being disqualified at moderation. What a tutor can do is act like a supervisor: reviewing the research question for focus, checking argument structure and sourcing, and flagging where analysis has slipped into description. Useful EE support looks like short, regular check-ins rather than long sessions, because the actual writing has to remain the student's own work throughout. If a tutor offers to 'help write' sections directly, that is a warning sign worth acting on immediately.

faqs.question: Does online tutoring really work for a subject like HL Maths?
faqs.answer: It depends on the subject more than on online tutoring generally. HL Maths, sciences and economics work well online because a shared whiteboard and screen-annotated past papers cover most of what a lesson needs. Subjects with heavy discussion, like some Language A or Individuals and Societies courses, still work online but benefit from a tutor deliberately building in more back-and-forth rather than lecturing at a screen. Where online genuinely struggles is with a student who needs physical presence to stay focused — that is a real limitation, and home or hybrid tutoring usually serves that student better.

faqs.question: What happens if my child's predicted grade doesn't move?
faqs.answer: First, a specific look at why — is it exam technique, gaps in one topic, or something with the IA and mocks pulling the average down. A predicted grade that has not moved after a reasonable stretch, usually six to eight weeks, is worth raising directly with the tutor rather than waiting through the term. Sometimes the fix is more session frequency; sometimes it is the wrong tutor for that specific subject and level. IB Gram treats a tutor change at that point as normal problem-solving, not as a failure of the plan or the student.

faqs.question: How much does an IB Diploma Programme tutor cost?
faqs.answer: Fees are set between the family and the individual tutor, and they vary by subject, level, tutor experience and session frequency, so there is no single number that applies across HL Physics, EE supervision and a Group 6 arts subject alike. It is reasonable to ask a shortlisted tutor for a written plan with a per-session rate and an estimate of total sessions before an exam session, rather than agreeing verbally. Comparing that plan against what a specific problem actually needs — one weak topic versus a full six-subject overhaul — usually matters more than comparing headline rates alone.

faqs.question: Can we change tutors partway through the year?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is more common than families expect — a subject mismatch or a personality mismatch usually surfaces a few sessions in, not on day one. IB Gram supports moving to a different tutor without treating it as starting over; the school feedback, mock results and diagnostic notes from the first attempt carry over and usually make the second match faster. Waiting through a poor fit to avoid an awkward conversation is the more expensive choice, since exam-session timelines do not pause while a mismatch gets tolerated.

faqs.question: Is home tutoring available everywhere, or only in certain cities?
faqs.answer: Home tutoring depends entirely on a tutor already being local to the family, so it is available in some cities and not others, and coverage tends to cluster where several IB schools sit close together. Online tutoring is available worldwide regardless of city, run in the family's own time zone, which is why most DP families end up using it for at least one subject even if they also arrange home tutoring for another. If home tutoring is not available locally, a hybrid plan — online for the subject, occasional in-person catch-ups if a tutor is ever nearby — is usually the realistic middle option.

faqs.question: How soon before May or November exams should we start?
faqs.answer: Earlier is easier, but a late start is not wasted if the goal is scoped honestly. Beginning in year one, well before IA deadlines and mocks land in year two, gives a tutor time to build subject depth rather than just patch gaps. Starting six to ten weeks before a May or November session still works for closing a specific, identified weakness — a shaky topic, exam technique under time pressure — but it is not realistic for rebuilding an entire subject from a low base in that window, and a straightforward tutor will say so rather than overpromise.

faqs.question: Will the tutor coordinate with my child's school or IB coordinator?
faqs.answer: Tutors are encouraged to work from whatever the school's IB coordinator has already provided — IA rubric comments, mock exam papers, the current predicted grade — rather than starting from a blank syllabus outline. IB Gram itself has no relationship with any school or its coordinator and does not contact schools directly; that channel stays between the family and the school. What a tutor can do is ask the family to bring that feedback into sessions, since it is usually more precise than a general 'weak in this subject' description and saves time that would otherwise go into re-diagnosing something already known.

faqs.question: Is IB Gram affiliated with the IB Organization?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram is an independent tutoring platform and has no official affiliation with the IB Organization, Cambridge International or Pearson Edexcel. It does not set the DP syllabus, mark any assessment, or speak on behalf of any exam board — it matches families with tutors who are familiar with how those bodies structure and assess the Diploma Programme. Any claim of official partnership from a tutoring platform is worth double-checking directly with the exam board in question, since IB Gram makes no such claim and structures its service accordingly.

contentBlocks.heading: What a Parent Is Actually Looking For at This Stage
contentBlocks.body: Type 'IB Middle Years Programme tutors' into a search bar and most results look interchangeable: same stock photography, same promise of results. What actually changes a Year 4 or Year 5 outcome is narrower than that. A tutor needs to know how the subject-group criteria are worded in the current MYP guide, how command terms like 'discuss' or 'justify' differ from 'describe', and how a school's own rubric maps onto the general IB descriptors. Parents searching for help usually arrive after one of three moments: a criterion score drops between units, a report comment mentions inconsistent achievement across strands, or the personal project or interdisciplinary unit is due and the student has frozen. None of these are fixed by generic revision. They are fixed by someone reading the actual task sheet with the student, identifying which strand is weak, and building two or three weeks of targeted practice around it. That is a slower, less flashy process than a marketing page usually admits. It also means the first conversation with a tutor should be about the student's actual assessment criteria, not a sales pitch about results. IB Gram's matching process below is built around that distinction, and it is worth reading before comparing tutors on price alone, because the wrong subject match at a lower rate rarely saves money once a term has been lost to it.
items: Criterion score drop between units
Report comment on inconsistent strand achievement
Personal project or interdisciplinary unit stalling
Generic revision that does not target the rubric

contentBlocks.heading: How IB Gram Pairs a Student With a Tutor
contentBlocks.body: Matching starts with specifics, not a general request for 'an MYP tutor'. A parent shares the year group, the subject or subjects, the school's assessment calendar if known, and whatever is already causing concern, whether that is a specific criterion, a personal project deadline or a pattern of rushed homework. From there, IB Gram checks a tutor's subject background, familiarity with the MYP framework for that subject group, and prior experience with the relevant year band, since teaching a Year 1 student is a different skill from preparing a Year 5 student for the transition into the Diploma Programme or an equivalent senior programme. A short compatibility check follows: teaching style, language of instruction if relevant, and scheduling fit across time zones for online families. The first session itself is diagnostic rather than instructional. A competent tutor spends it reading recent work, asking the student to talk through a recent assessment task in their own words, and identifying which command terms or criteria strands are the actual gap, rather than assuming the whole subject is the problem. Parents should expect a short written note after that first session: what was found, what the plan for the next four weeks looks like, and how progress will be checked. If that note does not arrive, that is a fair reason to ask why, and a fair reason to request a different tutor if the fit still feels wrong after two sessions.

contentBlocks.heading: Where MYP Sits Between PYP and the Diploma
contentBlocks.body: The Middle Years Programme covers the years between the Primary Years Programme and the Diploma Programme or Career-related Programme, generally spanning early adolescence through the start of upper secondary, though the exact age band a school assigns to each MYP year varies. Assessment across MYP is criterion-related rather than purely marks-based: each subject group has its own set of criteria, typically labelled A through D, and a student's grade for a unit reflects performance against each strand, not a single averaged score. This is the detail generalist tutors most often miss, because it means a student can write fluently and still lose marks on a criterion they were not addressing at all. Tutoring support that ignores this structure tends to produce essays that read well but do not move the actual grade, which is a frustrating and avoidable outcome. Toward the end of MYP, schools that continue into the Diploma Programme expect a smoother transition if the personal project has been handled seriously, since it previews the independent research skills the Extended Essay will later demand. Families sometimes ask whether it is worth investing in MYP tutoring at all if the Diploma Programme is still two years away. The honest answer is that habits formed in Year 4 and Year 5, particularly around citing sources correctly and structuring an extended piece of writing, are exactly what determine how smoothly the IA and EE process goes later, so the investment is rarely wasted.

Criterion-related grading, strands A through D
Personal project previews Extended Essay skills

contentBlocks.heading: Online, Home or a Mix: What Actually Fits
contentBlocks.body: Online tutoring is available worldwide and runs in the family's own time zone, which matters more for MYP families than it might first appear, since it means a strong tutor for a less common subject combination does not have to live in the same city, or even the same country. Home tutoring depends on tutor availability in the family's city and tends to suit younger MYP students, roughly Years 1 through 3, who benefit from a fixed physical routine and less screen time after a full school day. Hybrid arrangements, combining a weekly in-person session with online check-ins between them, work well when a family wants the discipline of a set appointment but also needs flexibility around school trips, illness or exam-period scheduling changes. None of these modes is universally better. A Year 5 student preparing intensively for the personal project may do better with a specialist tutor found online than with a generalist available locally. A Year 1 student still building study habits may do better with a home tutor who can sit alongside them and model how to organise a workbook. It is worth being honest that online tutoring asks more of the student's own initiative between sessions, since there is no adult physically present to notice a distracted afternoon, and some younger students genuinely need that physical presence for the first year or two before online works well for them.
items: Online: worldwide, family's own time zone
Home: depends on tutor availability, suits Years 1-3
Hybrid: weekly in-person plus online check-ins
Online needs more student self-initiative between sessions

contentBlocks.heading: Subject Depth Across the MYP Groups
contentBlocks.body: MYP organises learning into eight subject groups: Language and Literature, Language Acquisition, Individuals and Societies, Sciences, Mathematics, Arts, Physical and Health Education, and Design. A tutor's usefulness depends heavily on which of these groups the concern sits in, because the assessment criteria differ meaningfully between them. Language and Literature criteria reward analysis of how a writer's choices create effect; Individuals and Societies criteria often reward investigating and communicating with named sources; Design criteria are built around a design cycle of inquiry, ideation, planning and evaluation that has almost nothing in common with how a Sciences criterion is structured. A tutor strong in one group is not automatically useful in another, even within the same broad subject area, which is why IB Gram matches on the specific subject group and criteria set rather than a generic label like 'MYP tutor'. Mathematics and Sciences tutoring at this stage tends to focus on applying concepts to unfamiliar contexts, since MYP assessment deliberately avoids pure recall questions. Language Acquisition support depends heavily on the phase the student is working in, since a Phase 1 learner and a Phase 5 learner are doing almost unrelated work. Parents who are not sure which subject group is the actual problem, as opposed to which subject, should say so during matching. It is a normal question, and naming the uncertainty upfront leads to a better first tutor match than guessing.
items: Language and Literature: analysing writer's choices
Individuals and Societies: investigating with sources
Sciences and Mathematics: applying concepts in context
Design: inquiry, ideation, planning, evaluation cycle
Language Acquisition: matched to the student's phase

contentBlocks.heading: What MYP Schools Expect That a Family Cannot See From Home
contentBlocks.body: Every school delivering the Middle Years Programme sets its own internal assessment calendar, moderates its own criterion grades against the general IB descriptors, and applies its own academic honesty policy for citing sources and using AI tools in coursework. None of this is visible to a parent unless the school shares it directly, which means a tutor who assumes a generic MYP structure can miss school-specific requirements that materially affect a grade. A responsible tutor asks to see the actual task sheet and rubric a school has issued, rather than working from a general MYP guide alone, and flags immediately if school-specific instructions conflict with general academic honesty expectations. IB Gram is an independent tutoring platform and is not officially affiliated with the IB Organization, Cambridge International or Pearson Edexcel, and does not claim to represent any individual school's policies. Families should treat a tutor's role as supporting the school's own assessment process, not replacing it or second-guessing a teacher's marking without first checking the rubric together. Where a family is unsure what their school expects for the personal project, an interdisciplinary unit or a specific criterion, that is a legitimate question to raise with the school directly, and a good tutor will say so rather than guessing on the family's behalf. This distinction matters more in MYP than it did in earlier years of school, because criterion-related assessment is genuinely bespoke to each school's implementation of the programme.
items: School sets its own internal assessment calendar
Academic honesty policy varies by school
Task sheet and rubric checked before planning starts
IB Gram is independent of the IB Organization, Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel

contentBlocks.heading: Home and Hybrid Availability by City
contentBlocks.body: Because IB Gram matches families with tutors worldwide, most Middle Years Programme support happens online and is not tied to any one country or market. Home and hybrid options exist wherever a suitable tutor is already local to a family, and that availability changes city by city and shifts over time as tutors join or move. Among the cities where families have found local tutors for home or hybrid MYP sessions are Ahmedabad, Bangalore, Bhopal, Bhubaneswar, Chandigarh, Chennai, Coimbatore, Dehradun, Delhi, Faridabad, Ghaziabad and Greater Noida, alongside online-only matches for families anywhere else in the world. A family in one of these cities who wants an in-person component should say so during matching, since it narrows the tutor pool to those who can realistically travel to the student, and travel time and traffic in a large city can make an otherwise well-matched tutor impractical for a weekly evening slot. A family outside these cities, or with no listed local tutors at all nearby, loses nothing by defaulting to online, since the subject and criteria match matters more than geography for MYP-level work. It is worth being direct about a limitation here: home tutoring supply in any one city depends on which tutors currently live and travel there, so it can be thinner for a less common subject combination than for a widely requested one like Mathematics or English.

contentBlocks.heading: What 'Vetted' Should Actually Mean
contentBlocks.body: 'Vetted' is a word that appears on almost every tutoring page and means very little without specifics. For IB Gram, it means a tutor's subject background is checked against the year group and subject group they are being matched to teach, that prior experience with MYP's criterion-related structure is confirmed rather than assumed from a general teaching background, and that references or verifiable teaching history are reviewed before a tutor is offered to a family. It does not mean a guaranteed grade, a guaranteed criterion level, or a promised improvement of any specific size, and any page that offers those numbers for MYP work should be treated with real suspicion, since criterion-related assessment does not move in predictable increments the way a percentage score might. What a family should reasonably expect instead is transparency: a written note after the first session describing what was found, a plan for the following weeks with specific criteria or command terms named, and a check-in around the four-week mark comparing the student's work against that plan. If progress has not moved by then, on either a specific criterion or general confidence with a command term, that is the point to ask direct questions, request a different tutor, or adjust the plan, rather than continuing on faith for a full term. A trust relationship that cannot be checked at the four-week mark is not really trust, it is just optimism.
items: Subject background checked against year and subject group
No guaranteed grades or criterion levels
Written note after every first session
Four-week check-in against the original plan

contentBlocks.heading: Checking a Tutor's Fit Before You Commit
contentBlocks.body: Before committing to a term of MYP tutoring, a parent can reasonably ask to see how a tutor plans to approach the specific subject group and year in question, not just a general CV. A tutor confident in their MYP background should be able to name the relevant criteria strands for the subject without prompting, describe roughly how many sessions a typical concern in that area takes to shift, and explain how they would handle a mismatch between what the school's rubric says and what a general MYP guide says, since those two sources do occasionally read differently. It is fair to ask what happens if the fit is wrong. IB Gram's process allows a family to request a different tutor if the first one or two sessions do not feel right, without treating that as a failure on the family's part, because subject knowledge and teaching style are two separate things and a tutor can have one without the other. Verification also runs the other way: a tutor should ask the parent for the actual task sheet, recent feedback from the school, and the student's own account of where they feel stuck, rather than starting with generic worksheets. A first month that produces no written feedback, no reference to the actual school rubric, and no specific plan is a reasonable signal to pause and ask what is actually happening in the sessions, before another month passes on the same pattern.
items: Ask for the specific criteria strands, not a general CV
Request the actual school rubric, not a generic worksheet
Switch tutors without penalty in the first two sessions
No written feedback in month one is a warning sign

contentBlocks.heading: Starting This Term Rather Than Next
contentBlocks.body: The best time to start MYP tutoring is usually right after a specific concern appears, not at the end of term when a report has already been written and the window to fix a criterion score has closed. Starting mid-unit is not a problem: a tutor can pick up an in-progress task sheet as easily as a fresh one, and in some ways a live assessment gives clearer information about the actual gap than a retrospective review of an old one would. Getting started does not require choosing a subject, a year group and a schedule all at once. Sharing what is known so far, even if that is only 'Year 4, Individuals and Societies, criterion B seems to be the issue', is enough for IB Gram to suggest a first match. From there the diagnostic first session, the four-week check-in and the option to request a different tutor if needed all follow the same process described above, whether the family is in a city with local tutors available or relying entirely on online sessions. A short delay while comparing tutors is normal and sensible. A long delay while waiting for the 'right' moment usually just means another unit passes with the same unresolved gap, which is the actual cost worth weighing against the time it takes to have one matching conversation now.
items: Share what is known, even if incomplete
Diagnostic session comes first
Mid-unit start is fine, often clearer than a fresh start
Four-week check-in follows automatically

faqs.question: How much does IB Middle Years Programme tutoring cost?
faqs.answer: Fees depend on the tutor's experience, the subject group, the year level and whether sessions are online, home or hybrid, so there is no single number that applies to every family. What IB Gram can commit to is transparency before a term starts: the rate for the specific tutor matched to your child is confirmed upfront, not adjusted mid-term, and there is no obligation to continue past an initial session if the match does not feel right. Home tutoring in cities with limited local supply for a subject tends to cost more than online tutoring for the same subject, simply because fewer tutors are available to travel.

faqs.question: Can we change tutors if the first one is not a good fit?
faqs.answer: Yes. If the first one or two sessions do not feel right, whether that is teaching style, pacing or subject depth, you can request a different tutor without it being treated as a complaint against the first one. Subject knowledge and teaching style are separate skills, and a tutor can be strong in one without suiting your child in the other. It helps to be specific about what did not work, since a second match is more likely to succeed with concrete feedback than with a general 'it wasn't right'. There is no fixed limit on how many times a family can ask to switch.

faqs.question: Does online tutoring actually work for MYP, or does a student need someone in the room?
faqs.answer: For most MYP subjects, yes, provided the student has a reasonably reliable internet connection and is willing to engage without an adult physically present. Online tutoring gives access to a specialist in a specific subject group or language phase regardless of where that tutor happens to live, which matters for less common subject combinations. It tends to ask more of the student's own initiative between sessions, since there is no one in the room to notice a distracted afternoon. Younger MYP students, roughly Years 1 to 2, sometimes do better starting with home tutoring and moving to online once study habits are established.

faqs.question: What happens if there is no progress after a month?
faqs.answer: If a specific criterion or command term has not moved by the four-week check-in, that is the point to ask direct questions rather than continuing on faith. It can mean the tutor and student are not communicating well despite good subject knowledge, that the original diagnosis of the problem was wrong, or that the pace needs to change. IB Gram treats this as a normal part of the process, not a failure, and a different tutor or a revised plan can be requested at that point. What should not happen is a full term passing with no written note and no visible change in the actual assessed work.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with the personal project without doing the work for the student?
faqs.answer: A tutor can guide the process, questions and inquiry cycle behind the personal project without producing the work itself, since academic honesty rules apply to tutoring support the same way they apply to any other outside help. That usually looks like helping the student narrow a broad idea into something actually researchable, checking that sources are being recorded and cited as the process goes rather than at the end, and reviewing drafts against the specific criteria before submission. A tutor who offers to write sections of the project, or to heavily rewrite a student's own work, is not something IB Gram supports or arranges.

faqs.question: Our school's rubric looks different from the general MYP criteria descriptors. Which one does the tutor follow?
faqs.answer: The school's own rubric always takes priority, because it is what the student will actually be assessed against, and schools sometimes phrase or weight the general MYP criteria descriptors slightly differently in their internal documents. A tutor should ask to see that specific rubric before planning sessions rather than working from a general IB guide alone. Where the two genuinely conflict, or where a family is unsure which one governs a particular task, that question belongs with the school directly, and a good tutor will say so rather than guessing on the family's behalf or contradicting a teacher's stated expectations.

faqs.question: Is IB Gram affiliated with the IB Organization?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram is an independent tutoring platform and is not officially affiliated with the IB Organization, Cambridge International or Pearson Edexcel. Tutors matched through IB Gram are checked for subject knowledge and familiarity with the MYP framework, but IB Gram does not set, moderate or influence any school's grades, and does not speak on behalf of the IB Organization or any individual school. Families should treat tutoring as a support alongside the school's own teaching and assessment, not a substitute for it, and should direct any questions about official grading or moderation to the school itself.

faqs.question: What age or year group is MYP tutoring appropriate for?
faqs.answer: MYP spans several years between the Primary Years Programme and the Diploma Programme or an equivalent senior programme, with the exact age band for each MYP year set by the individual school. Tutoring support is available across that full range, from early MYP years focused on building study habits and subject fluency through to the final years where the personal project and preparation for the transition into senior study become the focus. The right starting point depends on the specific year group and subject concern rather than age alone, so sharing the actual MYP year during matching gets a more accurate tutor fit.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with more than one MYP subject group?
faqs.answer: Yes, though a tutor strong in one subject group is not automatically strong in another, even within a related subject area, since the assessment criteria and command terms differ meaningfully between groups. A family needing support across more than one subject, for example both Sciences and Individuals and Societies, may be matched with one tutor confident across both or with two specialists, depending on what is available and what actually suits the student's schedule. It is worth naming every subject of concern during matching rather than raising the second one later, since it can change which tutors are realistic options.

faqs.question: Do sessions run in our own time zone if we book an online tutor?
faqs.answer: Yes. Online sessions are scheduled in the family's own time zone rather than the tutor's, which matters for families whose tutor happens to be matched from a different part of the world for a specialist subject or language phase. Scheduling is agreed directly between the family and tutor during matching, including around school timings, exam periods and internal assessment deadlines, so sessions land at a time that actually works for the student rather than a generic slot. This flexibility is one of the clearer advantages online tutoring has over a fixed weekly home visit.

h1: IB Primary Years Programme Tutors for Reading, Maths and Exhibition Support
heroTitle: PYP Tutoring Built Around This Term's Unit, Not an Exam
heroSubtitle: A tutor who knows there's no May or November exam in PYP, working on reading, number sense and Exhibition research inside whatever unit of inquiry your child's class is currently covering, whether that's early literacy at age six or Exhibition planning at eleven.
introSummary: IB Primary Years Programme tutors help with the actual shape of PYP learning: reading and number-sense development, writing structure, and support for the units of inquiry a child's class is currently working through, plus the PYP Exhibition in the final year. Unlike the Diploma Programme, PYP has no May or November exam sitting and no past papers to practise — assessment happens through classroom observation and end-of-unit summative tasks instead. IB Gram matches families with tutors experienced specifically in this age band and framework, for online sessions worldwide, or home tutoring depending on tutor availability nearby.

contentBlocks.heading: What's Actually Due This Term, and Why 'Falling Behind' Means Something Different Here
contentBlocks.body: Ask what's due in the Primary Years Programme and the honest answer is: nothing that looks like an IB exam, because PYP has none. There's no May or November exam sitting the way there is in the Diploma Programme, no Paper 1 or Paper 2, no single external mark that decides anything. What exists instead is a school year built around roughly six units of inquiry, each running four to eight weeks around a central idea — a big transdisciplinary concept like 'systems have parts that interact' — explored through lines of inquiry in subjects like maths, language and social studies together, and closed out with a summative task the class works toward the whole unit. That task, not an exam, is what 'due this term' actually means for a PYP student most of the year. In the final year of the programme, students take on the PYP Exhibition, a term-long collaborative inquiry project that functions as the programme's one genuine capstone moment. So 'how late is too late to start tutoring' has a different answer here than it would for Diploma Biology. Joining three weeks into a unit means missing the provocation activity and the vocabulary the class built together, which a tutor can rebuild, but joining a week before the Exhibition presentation is a much tighter window, because that project's research and structure are meant to be built over months, not days.
items: No May or November exam sitting in PYP — that structure belongs to the Diploma Programme
Roughly six units of inquiry per year, each 4-8 weeks long
Each unit ends in a summative task, not a test
Final year: the PYP Exhibition, a term-long collaborative project
Joining mid-unit is recoverable; joining just before Exhibition presentations is not

contentBlocks.heading: Reading, Number Sense and the Eight Concepts That Sit Under Every Unit
contentBlocks.body: PYP tutoring covers the same building blocks any primary-age tutoring would — reading fluency and comprehension, number sense, written expression — but it teaches them differently, because PYP doesn't separate subjects the way a traditional primary curriculum does. Maths and language skills get taught inside a unit of inquiry's central idea rather than as standalone lessons, so a tutor working on multiplication with a Grade 3 student might frame it inside that term's unit on how communities organise resources, using the same vocabulary the classroom teacher is using. The programme also runs on key concepts — form, function, causation, change, connection, perspective, responsibility and reflection — that repeat across every unit and every year, and a tutor who understands which concept a current unit is built on can help a student see the pattern rather than treating each unit as an unrelated topic. Underneath all of this sits the IB Learner Profile — attributes like inquirer, thinker, communicator — which shapes how work gets framed and discussed even when it's never explicitly graded. A common mismatch: parents used to a more traditional curriculum sometimes want drilling on isolated maths facts or spelling lists, while the school wants inquiry-based thinking. The honest answer is a student usually needs both, and a tutor who refuses to do any rote practice because it isn't 'inquiry enough' is being precious about method at the student's expense.
items: Reading fluency, comprehension and number sense, taught through the unit's central idea
Key concepts recur across every unit: form, function, causation, change, connection, perspective, responsibility, reflection
The IB Learner Profile shapes how work is discussed, even when ungraded
Maths and language often taught inside a unit's theme, not as standalone lessons
Some rote practice alongside inquiry-based work is usually still needed

contentBlocks.heading: Matching a Tutor to a Seven-Year-Old Is a Different Problem Than Matching One to a Teenager
contentBlocks.body: Matching for PYP starts from the child's age and current unit, not from an exam board or a syllabus document, because there isn't one in the DP sense. IB Gram asks what unit of inquiry the class is currently working through, which specific skill is the actual concern — reading below grade level, number sense that hasn't clicked, or general support ahead of the Exhibition — and how the child responds to structure versus open-ended tasks, because that shapes which tutor's style will actually land. A tutor matched to a six-year-old needs a different temperament than one matched to a ten-year-old finishing Exhibition research, even if both are technically 'PYP tutors.' The first session looks less like a diagnostic test and more like a short working session plus a conversation with the parent about what a typical school week actually involves, because PYP classrooms vary a lot between schools in how much homework, structure and formal assessment they use. From that, a tutor proposes what the next month looks like — usually a mix of core skill practice and support that echoes whatever unit is currently running — rather than a fixed twelve-week syllabus, since PYP itself doesn't have one to follow. If the pace or personality isn't right, especially with younger children where rapport matters as much as content, a different tutor can be requested without it being treated as unusual.
items: Matching starts from the child's age and current unit of inquiry
The specific concern is identified: reading, number sense, or Exhibition support
Tutor temperament matters as much as subject knowledge at this age
First session includes a conversation with the parent about the school's actual routine
A month-by-month plan, not a fixed syllabus — PYP doesn't have one to follow

contentBlocks.heading: Where a Tutor Can Actually Visit, and Where Online Is the Only Realistic Option
contentBlocks.body: For a programme like PYP, where the student is young, the online-versus-home decision carries more weight than it does for an older DP student who can manage a screen independently. Online tutoring is available worldwide, run in the family's own time zone, and works well for reading and maths practice once a child is old enough to sit through a video session with reasonable focus — typically from around age seven or eight, though this varies hugely by child. Home tutoring depends entirely on a tutor already being active in or near a given city, so it can be requested but not promised. In cities including Ahmedabad, Bangalore, Bhopal, Bhubaneswar, Chandigarh, Chennai, Coimbatore, Dehradun, Delhi, Faridabad, Ghaziabad and Greater Noida, families can ask whether a home-visiting tutor is currently available for PYP-age children; this shifts month to month and gets confirmed only at the matching stage. For a five- or six-year-old, home tutoring is often simply more practical — shorter attention spans do better with a person in the room who can adjust the pace mid-session in ways a screen makes harder. A family in one of these cities but in a location that's genuinely difficult for a tutor to reach regularly, because of traffic or distance, may still end up choosing online even for a younger child, purely as the more reliable option week to week.
items: Online tutoring: worldwide, in the family's own time zone
Home tutoring: depends on a tutor already active in or near the city
Cities with potential home-tutor availability include Ahmedabad, Bangalore, Chennai, Delhi and Chandigarh
Younger children (roughly under 7-8) often do better with in-person sessions
Distance or traffic can make online the more reliable weekly option even for younger children

contentBlocks.heading: The Runway From PYP Into MYP and Diploma
contentBlocks.body: PYP covers programme-specific age bands rather than the fixed grade numbers used later in schooling — broadly early years through to around age twelve, ending in what most schools call Grade 5, right before the Middle Years Programme begins. Because the age band is wide, what 'PYP tutoring' means for a five-year-old and for an eleven-year-old finishing the programme are barely comparable jobs. Early on, it's mostly about foundational literacy and numeracy delivered with enough flexibility that a tutor can follow a child's actual pace rather than a fixed script. By the last one or two years of PYP, the work starts to resemble study skills more than direct teaching — organising Exhibition research, structuring a piece of extended writing, learning to plan backward from a deadline — because these are exactly the habits MYP will expect immediately, without much of a transition period. Families sometimes treat the PYP-to-MYP shift as a small step; teachers who've watched the transition tend to describe it as sharper than that, mostly because MYP introduces separate subject teachers, formal criteria-based grading and considerably more independent work all at once. A student who leaves PYP already comfortable with a bit of structured independence — planning their own study time, checking their own work against a set of expectations — adjusts to that shift with noticeably less friction than one who leaves PYP purely used to open-ended inquiry with heavy adult scaffolding.
items: PYP runs across early years to around age twelve, ending in Grade 5 at most schools
Early PYP: foundational literacy and numeracy at the child's own pace
Later PYP: study skills — planning, structuring writing, backward-planning from deadlines

contentBlocks.heading: Vetting Looks Different When the Student Is Six, Not Sixteen
contentBlocks.body: Vetting a tutor for a seven-year-old is not the same exercise as vetting one for a seventeen-year-old preparing for Paper 3, and IB Gram treats it that way. The core checks still apply — genuine subject grounding in early literacy and numeracy pedagogy, and familiarity with how the IB Primary Years Programme actually works, its units of inquiry, key concepts and Learner Profile, rather than generic 'kids' tutoring dressed up with IB language. But for this age group, conduct and manner matter proportionally more: patience under repetition, the ability to keep a young child's attention without resorting to bribery-as-teaching-method, and a basic understanding of how to work respectfully and safely with a minor. None of this is published as a numeric score, but it can be discussed directly with a parent before a match is confirmed, and a parent is entitled to ask specific questions about a proposed tutor's experience with this exact age band before agreeing to a first session. What verification does not promise is a particular reading level by a particular date or a guaranteed jump in maths ability — young children develop unevenly, sometimes in bursts, and no amount of tutor qualification changes that basic fact about how children learn. What it does promise is that the person sitting with your child has a real, checkable background in both the subject matter and in working with children this age, not just one or the other.

Grounding in early literacy and numeracy pedagogy specifically
Conduct and manner checked with extra weight for this age group
No guaranteed reading level or maths jump by a set date
Specific questions about a tutor's experience with this age band are welcome before booking

contentBlocks.heading: Screen Time, Attention Span and Which Mode Actually Works at This Age
contentBlocks.body: The online-versus-home question for PYP-age children isn't really about geography first; it's about attention span and screen tolerance, and geography second. Online tutoring gives access to a specialist PYP tutor regardless of city, which matters because good PYP-specific tutoring experience isn't evenly distributed even within one city, let alone available everywhere a family might live. It works well for structured skill practice in short, well-paced sessions, and plenty of eight- and nine-year-olds manage this fine once a tutor has learned how to keep a screen session moving. It works less well for a five- or six-year-old who needs frequent redirection, physical materials — counters, letter tiles, a shared page to actually write on together — or simply someone in the room to notice when focus has genuinely gone rather than reading it off a video feed with a slight lag. Home tutoring suits these younger learners better for exactly that reason, and also suits families near enough to a tutor's travel route that regular in-person sessions are realistic rather than occasional. Hybrid plans are common here too: a home-based tutor for the youngest, most attention-fragile stretch, shifting to online once the child is old enough to sustain a session independently, often somewhere around the upper years of the programme. There's no fixed age where this switch should happen — it depends entirely on the individual child, and a good tutor says so honestly rather than pushing a preferred mode regardless of fit.
items: Online: access to specialist PYP tutors regardless of city
Online works less well for children needing frequent redirection or physical materials
Home tutoring suits younger, more attention-fragile learners
Hybrid: home-based early on, shifting to online as independence grows
The right age to switch modes depends on the individual child, not a fixed rule

contentBlocks.heading: PYP Looks Different at Every School — Tutoring Has to Follow That, Not Fight It
contentBlocks.body: No two schools run the Primary Years Programme identically, even though they're all authorised against the same IB framework. Some schools set formal homework and weekly spelling lists on top of their units of inquiry; others deliberately avoid anything that looks like traditional homework in the early years, trusting the inquiry process itself to build the skills. A tutor who assumes one version of PYP is universal will misjudge what a family actually needs, which is why the first real question in any PYP tutoring relationship is simply what this particular school does, not what PYP does in general. IB Gram is an independent tutoring platform. It has no relationship with the IB Organization, no access to any school's internal planning documents, and no affiliation with Cambridge International or Pearson Edexcel, since those bodies aren't relevant to PYP in any case. A tutor's information about what's currently happening in class comes from the parent and the student, not from any privileged channel into the school, and a family should be a little wary of anyone implying otherwise. In practice, this means the first session or two often involves as much listening as teaching — understanding what the school's version of a unit of inquiry actually looks like on the ground, what the teacher has emphasised, and where the gaps genuinely are, before deciding what a tutor should spend time on.
items: No two schools run PYP identically, despite a shared IB framework
Some schools set formal homework; others avoid it in the early years by design
IB Gram has no relationship with the IB Organization or any school's internal planning
Not affiliated with Cambridge International or Pearson Edexcel
Early sessions involve real listening — understanding this school's specific version of PYP

contentBlocks.heading: Four Weeks In: The Signs That Actually Mean Something at This Age
contentBlocks.body: Because there's no test at the end of a PYP unit the way there's an exam at the end of a DP course, 'is this working' has to be judged on smaller, more visible signals. After four weeks, a parent should be able to point to something concrete: a child reading a slightly harder book without resistance, number facts recalled without finger-counting every time, a piece of writing with a clearer structure than the one from a month ago, or simply less friction around homework in the evening. If a parent can't name anything like that, it's worth asking the tutor directly what's actually been worked on and why, rather than assuming things are fine because the sessions are pleasant. Young children's progress is genuinely uneven and sometimes invisible for weeks before it shows up all at once — a child can seem stuck on blending sounds for a month and then suddenly read fluently within a week — so a single flat month isn't automatically a bad sign. What is a bad sign is a tutor who can't describe, specifically, what's been attempted and what's next. IB Gram does not publish invented reading-level jumps, average score improvements, or ratings for PYP tutoring, because at this age, progress depends heavily on the individual child's development, the school's own teaching, and consistency at home, not on a tutor's skill in isolation, however good that tutor is.
items: Concrete four-week signals: harder reading, faster recall, clearer writing, less homework friction
Ask the tutor directly what's been worked on if nothing feels visible
Young children's progress can be invisible for weeks, then sudden
A tutor who can't describe the plan specifically is the actual warning sign
No invented reading-level statistics or ratings published

contentBlocks.heading: The First Step Is a Conversation, Not a Long Enrolment Form
contentBlocks.body: Starting PYP tutoring doesn't require knowing exactly what's wrong first — that's often exactly what the first conversation is for. Share the child's age, the school's current unit of inquiry if you know it, and whatever the actual worry is, whether that's reading confidence, maths avoidance, or general nervousness about the upcoming Exhibition. IB Gram matches based on that, proposing a tutor whose age-group experience and temperament fit, for online sessions worldwide or home sessions where a tutor happens to be available nearby. Fees vary by tutor experience and session length, and are confirmed before any booking; there's no single flat rate, because a tutor experienced specifically with early literacy intervention is a different hire than a general primary tutor, and pricing reflects that honestly rather than pretending otherwise. If the Exhibition is close and the concern is specifically about that project, say so upfront, since the useful window for meaningful help narrows fast in the final weeks before presentations. There's no obligation to commit beyond a first session, and no assumption that PYP tutoring needs to run for a full year; some families want three or four sessions to fix one specific gap before it compounds, others want ongoing weekly support across a whole unit of inquiry or an entire school year. Both are normal, and the plan should be built around whichever is actually true for this child, not around a default package that assumes every family wants the same thing.
